# Callback Queue and Download Requirements History

## 2023-03-20: Starting Point

This page originally recorded two things together with 3.0.0-alpha.3: callback queue semantics and an unknown content-length download. Both were grouped under interface behavior that still needed to be revisited before closeout, but they came from different places, and there was not enough material to form a single set of rules.

The previous investigation started from `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h`. The remaining navigation points were `namespace internal {`, `class AnyMetadata;`, `struct TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto {`, and `class CBilling_Address;`, along with the adjacent `CBilling_AddressDefaultTypeInternal`, `CCDDBAppDetailCommon`, and `CCDDBAppDetailCommonDefaultTypeInternal`. These declarations can show the structure of the files that generate messages, but they cannot tie the callback pump, handler registry, or download read path back to this file.

At the time, both the issue name and the call name pointed to this file in order to leave a stable lookup entry as a starting point. That entry was later easy to read as the implementation location, so this version records "start looking here" and "behavior is determined here" separately.

## Initial Draft Decisions

The initial draft had two options. The first was to summarize callback handling, waiting, and the async entry point as a single callback dequeue operation; its advantage was a shorter history, but it flattened the result for an empty queue, how waiting ends, and how many items a single call consumes. The second was to record the input conditions, visible results, and consumption scope separately for each public entry point; its advantage was preserving the boundaries, but its drawback was exposing the lack of a conclusion on the download side.

The first option was adopted at the time. The download was recorded by title only; the unknown content-length download was not treated as a success path, nor was it directly labeled a transport failure. No command, environment, response sample, or caller result was preserved here, so an experiment cannot be reconstructed.

This is not a sufficiently good interface record. It conflated when to return with how many items are processed after returning, and it left no completion condition for the download issue that could be checked again. What needed changing later was the recording method and decision scope, not inferring the entire call chain from the generated header.

## Review Addendum

During review, the first question was what the caller could observe, followed by which directory held the implementation. The callback side was consequently split into three verification tracks: the return value of the normal runtime entry point, the termination behavior of the waiting entry point, and the dispatch cap for a single call to the async-wait entry point. The three tracks can share the queue object, but they cannot continue to share one ambiguous conclusion about processing completion.

This addendum provides no runtime output and does not claim that the three entry points have been reproduced in the same environment. It only establishes three questions to track separately in the next version: whether an empty queue can be identified from the return value, whether it ends cleanly when the wait expires, and whether a single async call continues on to consume a second item. The old single-action wording can still remain as historical material, but it can no longer serve as the basis for a decision.

The download side has no evidence of comparable strength. The review requirement was to check the unknown content-length download using the repository maintainer's routine steps, and to leave areas lacking evidence explicitly blank. An unknown length cannot automatically be recast as a particular exception, nor can the callback-side split be used to prove that the download can complete.

## Experiment Record: No Result

This verification left no citable command, CI job, environment, or failure output. The only things that can be confirmed are that the questions were split apart and that the download item remains pending review. "No result" is deliberately not rewritten as a failure here; a failure requires an input and an observed symptom, which the current material does not contain.

Likewise, class names in the generated header can only help a reader get back to the old entry point. `AnyMetadata` and `CBilling_Address` are locatable declarations, not runtime records of the callback queue. `TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto` also did not surface a download-reading object in the materials from this round.

## Legacy Paragraph Retained

> Callbacks can initially be understood as a single queue operation; if the waiting and async entry points are later found to produce different results, split them.

**Deprecated.** This was the initial draft's working assumption; it is retained to explain why the early material discussed only retrieving callbacks and did not distinguish the return value, wait termination, and consumption count. The post-review record no longer treats this sentence as the shared semantics for the three entry points.

## Decision Scope for This Version

- Investigate the three callback entry points separately; no longer use one umbrella term to stand in for their respective return and consumption behavior.
- `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h` remains a navigation point for the previous investigation; the generated declarations there cannot establish implementation ownership.
- Keep the unknown content-length download within review scope only; make no success or failure determination.

The next version needs to move the callback boundaries that can already be stated in interface terms farther down, while explaining why they still coexist with the download history on this page.

# History of Callback Queue and Download Requirements

## 2023-03-20: Starting from the Entry Point Left in the Generated Header Files

This page originally recorded two issues for 3.0.0-alpha.3 together: callback queue semantics, and unknown content-length download. Both were put in the pile of issues to revisit before development wrap-up, but they were not initially treated as part of the same implementation chain, nor were they backed by the same set of evidence from the actual environment.

The earlier investigation started at `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h`. The earliest notes preserved a few narrowly scoped reference points:

```text
namespace internal {
class AnyMetadata;
struct TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto {
class CBilling_Address;
class CBilling_AddressDefaultTypeInternal;
class CCDDBAppDetailCommon;
class CCDDBAppDetailCommonDefaultTypeInternal;
```

These names remained on the page, not because they later established ownership of the callbacks or downloads, but because they were local entry points that could be found again at the time. The file's local role was recorded as an existing h module, suitable for reading code and cross-checking historical behavior. Up to this point, the material only supported "starting from generated declarations", not "the generated declarations are the behavioral implementation".

At the time, both the issue names and call names pointed to this path. The benefit was that a search would not start with a title that had no associated file object, but the trade-off was that readers could easily mistake a navigation point for a caller or runtime object. This confusion recurred later, so this version does not interpret `internal`,`AnyMetadata` or `CBilling_Address` as a handler registry, callback pump or download read path.

## Initial Draft: Putting the Two Issues Together First

The initial goal of the notes was very limited: to preserve two topics that someone would revisit during the alpha.3 wrap-up, without rushing to turn them into a reference page. There were two options for the callback section.

The first approach described ordinary callback processing, processing with a wait and asynchronous waiting as a single action of retrieving a callback. Its advantage was brevity, and it kept the history and requirement titles in the same paragraph; the trade-off was that it hid three distinct boundaries actually visible to the caller. The observable outcome when the queue was empty would be conflated with wait expiration, and there was also no place to specify whether a single asynchronous call processed one item or continued retrieving the next one.

The second approach was to keep separate notes for each public entry point. Each entry point had at least three fields: the conditions at the time of the call, the result received by the caller, the queue work that might still remain after the call. This approach would expose the gaps on the download side in the document, and would also force maintainers to acknowledge that no single "processing complete" statement could stand in for all three entry points. The initial draft did not adopt it immediately, not because the first approach was considered more correct, but because the only intention at the time was to get the history down first.

The download task was phrased more briefly in the initial draft. unknown content-length download was retained only as a name and a follow-up item. The absence of content-length does not automatically mean failure, nor is there evidence that it can unconditionally finish via the success path. The initial draft did not preserve response samples, the reading process, commands, or caller results, so no decision was recorded for the download at that time.

> A callback can initially be understood as a queue operation; if it later turns out that the results of waiting and the async entry point differ, split them.

**Deprecated; retained as-is.** This was a working hypothesis from early 2023. It was not rewritten after the fact into a correct version, because it precisely explains why early search results so often contained only the fragments queue, empty, times, out, and one: the recorder first latched onto the action name, but did not preserve the return value and consumption count together.

## Review addendum: the question shifted from names to caller observations

Later review did not first ask for the complete source-code chain to be filled in; it first asked what each of the three entry points exposed to callers. The resulting split was not an implementation diagram; it was a layout decision for the interface record.

The standard run entry point must separately record a Boolean result. This prevents an empty queue from being ambiguously written as "nothing happened" or "keep waiting." The entry point with `TimeSpan` must separately record the waiting boundary, because a duration-bearing call and immediate processing are not the same action. The async entry point must also independently preserve the per-call consumption limit; it cannot be assumed to consume all the work that was in the queue at the time merely because it also handles callback.

The review addendum did not include runtime logs, nor did it claim that the three verification tracks had already been completed on the same batch of inputs. It only clearly listed the observation points that needed confirmation: the return value, deadline expiration, and single dispatch. This distinction is important. It allows the document to make a local decision, but does not allow the document to fabricate an experiment that was never preserved.

The source-code entry point was also repositioned in this round. `namespace internal {` indicates that the declaration is in the internal namespace of generated code; `class AnyMetadata;` and `class CBilling_Address;` indicate that the file does indeed contain the corresponding forward declarations; `TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto` indicates the naming form of the generated table structure. All of them can help navigate back to the file, but the scheduling rules of callback queue cannot be inferred from the names, much less can unknown content-length download be connected to this header file.

The record retained after the review was: if materials are added later, the caller-visible results for the three callback entry points should be sought separately; if download materials are added, the download's own inputs and completion observations should be saved from the actual download step. It did not turn "find the call edges next" into a cross-document evidence tutorial, nor did it use this gap as a substitute for the decision on this page.

## Recheck item: the download did not pass in the same round
The download portion did not achieve the same closure in review as the callback portion. The only inspection target left was the specific usage of unknown content-length download. What needs to be checked is not an abstract "whether the network is functioning normally," but what the download process actually relies on to know that reading has ended when content-length is missing, and what the caller treats as completion.

Here, there are no original commands, environment details, response headers, file results, or failure output that can be cited. Therefore, this page does not classify it as a transport-layer error, does not classify it as something that can complete normally via streaming, and does not infer a download conclusion from the behavior of the callback entry point. Leaving this item blank is a historical fact of this page, not the omission of a universal handling step.

This gap also explains why the two topics have continued to coexist. They were registered and revisited under the same alpha.3 requirements lineage, but the evidence objects differ: the callback topic could later be pinned down to the boundaries of three public entry points, while the download topic still has only a usage pattern and a verification entry point. Their coexistence does not mean shared implementation, failure cause, or owner.

## The old assessment left after 2023 years

Below is a passage that was not removed during later consolidation:

> The callback can initially be understood as a queue action; if it is later found that the results of waiting and the async entry differ, split them further.

It exists alongside the later split framing, and must not be read backwards. The old paragraph preserves the compressed formulation used at the time, while the later records preserve the post-review redivision of the externally observable surface. If only the old paragraph is read, empty-queue returns, the waiting deadline, and the async consumption count will be missed; if the old paragraph is rewritten in the later terms, it will erase why this page once had none of these fields.

Also left intact is the tendency to determine implementation ownership from the generated declaration. It is still possible to start tracing back from this path, but "searchable" and "already proven" are not the same thing. `CBilling_AddressDefaultTypeInternal`, `CCDDBAppDetailCommon`, and `CCDDBAppDetailCommonDefaultTypeInternal` continue to be retained as adjacent names in the file; they have not been expanded into a module responsibility table, nor have they been used to fill in the download item.

## A field record that did not produce a complete result

This page once needed a more complete review, but the result ultimately left behind was very limited. No CI job, version environment, or caller example could be included, so empty-queue behavior, waiting, and async dispatch cannot be written up as a field reproduction. What can be confirmed is that the review direction has changed from "which file does the issue name correspond to" to "what each entry point exposes to callers."

The same applies to the download. The lack of a response from content-length cannot, based on the title alone, be turned into an exception sample. Without the actual input being saved, it is impossible to tell whether streaming read, completion of writing to disk, or the caller's completion check was the first thing to go wrong. The unresolved item therefore remains documented as a scope, rather than a guessed root cause.

This section does not look like a traditional incident record because it is not an incident timeline; it preserves an interface review that did not produce complete output. This is retained to prevent later readers from misreading "no failure output" as "success has already been verified."

## Post-Review Appendix: Why Two Tracks Are Still Retained

After the organization associated with 2025-04-22, this history was not compressed into a one-page current specification. The maintainers confirmed at the time that the callback entry already had enough material to establish a caller-visible contract, while the download questions remained pending review; they are on the same page because they entered the record from the same batch of alpha.3 closeout items, not because a shared implementation was found later. The appendix continues to use this boundary to prevent the next round of organization from misrepresenting "placed together" as "handled by the same party".

The recording order for the callback track was also not changed to the implementation order. The normal runtime entry first answers what the caller gets when the queue is empty, the waiting entry then answers how the deadline ends, and the async entry finally answers the consumption scope of a single call. All three use the word queue, but they require different evidence: the return value must be assessed from the call result, the deadline from the end of the wait, and the consumption scope from the queue changes before and after a single call. The old draft combined all three precisely because it did not keep these observation targets separate.

### Why an Empty-Queue Record Cannot Replace a Wait Record

In the old note, "nothing happened" and "continue waiting for another round" once appeared next to each other. The review pointed out that these statements do not let the caller determine whether it was executing an immediate run or a wait with a deadline. An empty-queue record can only show that there was no dispatchable object before the call and what result the normal entry returned; it does not show how long the wait lasted or prove that the waiting entry took the same return branch. Conversely, a wait reaching its deadline cannot prove what the normal entry should return for an empty queue.

This separation later became a writing constraint for maintenance documentation: when recording evidence, the entry name, call condition, and visible result must appear in the same local paragraph. If only a single "queue is empty" log is preserved, it must still be labeled as incomplete evidence; if only one deadline expiration is preserved, it cannot be used to fill in the normal entry either. What is retained here is how to read the old material, not any new threads, locks, or scheduling mechanisms.

### The Single-Call Boundary of the Async Entry

The async entry can easily be pulled back into the old merged framing by the name "wait for callback". The review did not require the document to explain subsequent scheduling; it only required the observation scope of a single call to be explicit. Therefore, the review materials should retain the pending items visible before the call, the number actually dispatched by this call, and whether any objects remained in the queue after the call ended; this page must not infer who triggers the next call or in which synchronous context it continues.

No complete runtime output was left at the time, so the appendix does not fabricate a set of numbers. It only explains why the latest wording puts the per-call dispatch limit into the interface sentence, rather than casually writing "the queue will be emptied". If new caller samples appear later, each call should be recorded separately; the final total must not overwrite the intermediate boundaries, nor should the async entry's result replace evidence for the normal or waiting entry.

### Why Download Items Remain Open

The unknown content-length download has consistently lacked comparably strong runtime evidence in this material. The title indicates that usage without a length header is to be examined, but no response headers, configuration values, write results, or exception objects were saved. The review therefore refused to infer failure directly from "unknown length", or a complete download directly from "the connection eventually ended". To reach a decision, at a minimum, a single record must include which length values are available in the input, under what conditions reading ends, and what the caller ultimately receives.

This also limits how far the callback semantics can be extrapolated. A callback entry point's return and dispatch count cannot establish whether the download stream is complete, and the semantics of a wait expiring cannot serve as a termination condition for network reads either. The two tracks may appear next to each other on the release checklist, but they cannot share the same evidence of success or explanation of failure. There is currently no new runtime evidence for the download, so this part remains unresolved rather than being given a handling strategy just to make the history look complete.

### The generated header file serves only as a navigation aid

`Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h` appears in records from multiple rounds because it preserves a stable, searchable set of generated declarations. `internal`, `AnyMetadata`, `TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto`, and `CBilling_Address` can help maintainers confirm that they have returned to the same older material, but they do not show how the callback pump or downloader interacts at runtime. The appendix continues to present paths, declarations, and behavioral decisions in separate columns.

If a later search leads from this path to a new file, references and runtime evidence for the new relationship must be recorded at the target object; the search steps must not be rewritten to say that the header file had already called the target object. This restriction may seem conservative, but it preserves the chronological layers of the history: the early records did begin with generated declarations, while the later semantics came from interface reviews, and the two have different sources. Removing this distinction would make the old path look like proof of current behavior.

### Review excerpts from 2025-04-22

> First distinguish the results the caller sees, then discuss where the implementation belongs. The three types of entry points can share the problem context, but they cannot share a single completion statement.
>
> Keep the download item open if there is no runtime evidence; do not borrow a conclusion from another subproblem, and do not state that everything has already been fully written to disk just because no error was reported.
>
> Keep the old declaration path as an index. Put the current semantics in the later section, and explicitly mark that they were not derived from that path.

This excerpt explains why the latest version contains precise interface statements, a download item awaiting re-review, and an old source-code entry point at the same time. It does not add any new public behavior, but merely preserves in the document the choices made during the review. The original wording in the preceding section remains authoritative for the precise interface statements; they are not copied again here, to avoid having multiple similar versions compete with each other in search results.

### How to read this page at the next handoff

The person taking over should first confirm whether they are handling the callback track or the download track. The callback track starts from the later current wording, returns to the respective objects observed by the three entry points, and then checks as needed why the earlier draft merged them; the download track starts from the unresolved items and looks for new evidence that includes the input length, read completion, and caller result. Both tracks can use the historical index at the beginning of the page, but every new conclusion needs to be tied back to its own object.

If only one successful call is found, the old counterexamples or unresolved sections should not be deleted; if only one declaration is found, it should not be upgraded into an end-to-end relationship. A new review should append the date, object, and observable result, and indicate which old judgment it corrects. This way, the next revision will still show how the decision changed, rather than leaving only a final answer without a source.

There are still three gaps when closing out the appendix: the actual input for the download has not been filled in, the relationship between the generated header file and the actual implementation has not been restored on this page, and rescheduling after the asynchronous entry point is outside the current interface definition. Leave them in their respective sections rather than merging them into one broad TODO.

## 2025-04-22: Wording added later

The latestrevision corrected one specific old judgment: ordinary execution, execution with waiting, and asynchronous waiting can no longer be treated as the same kind of consumption operation. The interface requirements that can currently be retained publicly are as follows:

> CallbackManager.RunCallbacks() returns a boolean, reports false for an empty queue; RunWaitCallbacks(TimeSpan) times out cleanly and RunWaitCallbackAsync(CancellationToken) dispatches at most one callback. Contract revision repair-088-v1: public bool RunCallbacks(); public bool RunWaitCallbacks(TimeSpan timeout); public Task RunWaitCallbackAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default). Empty polling or an expired synchronous wait returns false. Each successful call consumes and dispatches at most one queued callback, returning true for the bool methods. Async waiting remains pending on an empty queue, cancellation throws OperationCanceledException without consuming a future callback, and a later call can still dispatch it. Callback subscriptions use the normal CallbackManager dispatch path.

This statement appears only once in this version, and is placed after at least four layers of older material. It is the current wording at the callback interface level, not an inference from the declaration of `steammessages_base.pb.h`. It brings three external boundaries that must be kept separate back into one place: the boolean return value and empty-queue result of the regular entry point, the wait deadline with `TimeSpan`, and the per-call dispatch limit of the asynchronous entry point.

The decisions here are still limited in scope. They do not specify handler registration order or the exception context, nor do they describe the connection lifecycle or who creates the queue. The asynchronous entry point's per-call limit also does not specify how subsequent calls are scheduled; how subsequent calls are triggered again is not covered in this material. A clean timeout at the entry point that waits also does not mean that download reading has finished; neither issue can stand in for the other.

## Record Boundary Table

| Object | Decisions already recorded | What still cannot be inferred from this page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regular callback entry point | Preserve the Boolean return value and retain the visible empty-queue branch | The handler implementation and the source of its registration |
| Entry point that waits | Preserve the boundary of a clean exit after `TimeSpan` expires | Thread scheduling and connection state during the wait |
| Asynchronous entry point that waits | Preserve the limit of dispatching at most one callback per call | How subsequent calls are scheduled, who triggers them again |
| Generated message header file | Serve as a local navigation aid for the earlier investigation | Inferring end-to-end call relationships from declarations |
| unknown content-length download | Preserve the usage details and pending-review status | Whether it succeeded, read completion conditions, and error types |

This table was added during later editing and was not part of the original draft. Its purpose is to place the boundaries of what the record can already establish alongside download questions that still lack evidence; it does not dress up gaps in the download material as callback rules or elevate source-code navigation points into runtime relationships.

## Meeting Excerpts and Adjacent Gaps

Two short excerpts remain from an earlier meeting:

> Don't write up "empty" as an exception yet. First confirm whether the caller gets a return value or the wait expires.
>
> Don't add a success conclusion for the unknown length item yet, as the on-site record is incomplete.

They are not complete meeting minutes, only a record of the shift in the discussion at the time. The first statement prompted the three-way callback classification, and the second explains why this page did not make a final determination on downloads. Neither statement provides implementation locations, test commands, or results, so they cannot be used to fill in any further background.

There is also an adjacent issue that has not been untangled: the earlier investigation used issue names and call names as search clues for navigating into the generated header file. This entry point is still useful for historical lookups, but similar names do not mean that relationships between the objects have been confirmed. If someone later uses that file to continue looking for the handler registry, callback pump, or download-reading code, the relationships will need to be established separately for the corresponding objects; this page does not disguise gaps as a complete call graph.

This also explains why this page retains two uneven sections of material. The callback material now has a later-added statement of interface behavior, the download material still only covers the scope pending review, and the source-code section still stops at a few declarations. They come from additions made at different times, and the layout has not been smoothed out again.

## Appendix: Old Examples Not Deleted

### Old Example A: Treating an Empty Queue as a Pre-Wait State

An early note described an empty queue as "just wait one more round". The original note did not preserve any test output or specify the corresponding entry point, so it is retained here only as a historical example. It was later superseded by the regular entry point's Boolean result and empty-queue boundary, so it cannot be used to guide current judgments. The value of retaining this item is that it shows why immediate execution and execution with waiting were initially grouped under the same action name.

### Old Example B: Directly Classifying Unknown Length as a Download Anomaly

Another old example placed unknown content-length download and failure handling on the same line, with no input, response, or result. At most, it shows that someone at the time treated the lack of a length as a signal to stop; it cannot prove that the download actually failed. This page also does not rewrite it into the opposite conclusion; what still needs review is the actual usage, the read-termination condition, and the caller's completion determination.

### Old Example C: Inferring Implementation Ownership from Generated Declarations

`AnyMetadata`, `TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto`, and `CBilling_Address` are easy-to-search declarations. They were not deleted because later readers may still use this path to return to the old records; nor were they expanded into a responsibility table, because the existing material only confirms the declaration locations and adjacent shape. What remains here is a search habit, not an implementation judgment.

## What This Page Ultimately Leaves Behind

The decisions in the history have two layers. The early material decided to put the two topics on the same page and left behind an over-merged callback assumption; the review material decided to split them by the return value visible to the caller, the deadline, and the scope of a single consumption; only the later consolidation preserved the precise wording for the three entry points. The download never obtained an actual result that could be added, so it remains an adjacent unresolved item on the same page.

`Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h` is still the entry point for the old investigation, and the generated declarations in the file can still be used for lookups, but this path cannot provide a complete explanation of the callback or download. When reading this page, the old paragraphs, review additions, resultless rechecks, later corrections, and old-example appendix should be treated separately; they are not different wordings of the same verification.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RunCallbacks
    RunCallbacks --> EmptyQueue: returns false
    [*] --> RunWaitCallbacks
    RunWaitCallbacks --> TimedOut: times out cleanly
    [*] --> RunWaitCallbackAsync
    RunWaitCallbackAsync --> OneCallback: dispatches at most one callback
```

The diagram only shows the boundaries of the three later interfaces. It does not connect the generated header files, the download read path, or the unconfirmed termination conditions to the state diagram; those remain in their respective historical sections.

# Ticket Ownership and PICS Review Plan

Review: we will no longer try a separate handler. PICS HTTP URI selection still has no sample calls, and URI remains unchanged.

A new SteamClient registers SteamAuthTicket by default and GetHandler<T>() returns that same handler for ticket status, acquisition, and cancellation callbacks. Contract revision repair-088-v1: public Task<SteamAuthTicket.TicketInfo> SteamAuthTicket.GetAuthSessionTicket(uint appid). TicketInfo implements IDisposable and exposes byte[] Ticket; Dispose cancels only that ticket and repeated disposal must not remove another ticket. A logged-in client first obtains SteamApps.GetAppOwnershipTicket(appid), then consumes a game-connect token, advertises the auth token through ClientAuthList and awaits its matching ClientAuthListAck TargetJobID. The ACK must contain the registered ticket CRC before acquisition succeeds. The returned bytes contain the auth token followed by a little-endian Int32 ownership-ticket length and the ownership-ticket bytes. Cancellation advertises the updated active list; identity is the same protocol CRC used for registration, not a CRC recomputed over the combined ticket. No login, unsuccessful ownership result, no token after ownership succeeds, or ACK missing the ticket CRC faults the acquisition Task with an Exception carrying that reason; exact exception subtype and wording are not prescribed. Game-connect token messages append tokens and keep at most max_tokens_to_keep (discard oldest); ClientLogOff clears unused tokens. SteamAuthTicket.TicketAcceptedCallback : CallbackMsg exposes List<uint> AppIDs, List<uint> ActiveTicketsCRC and uint MessageSequence. The earliest samples described just two cases. In one, after the callback returned, the result received by the outer layer did not match the expected text. There was no complete call stack, and the same object had not been saved both before and after the callback entered the queue.

The assessment recorded at the time was that the callback pump might have added another wrapper, and that jobid without a request might just be a log placeholder. That assessment stays here because it explains why the pump was investigated first at the time, not because it has since been proven correct. A single output cannot show which layer changed the value.

At the start of each investigation, record these fields together: callback type, received result, whether a request exists, and the jobid in the log. If there is a request, add its identifier from when it was sent; if there is no request, mark it only as a no-request sample. # Callback Results and Protocol Mask Troubleshooting Tree

This page was originally just a short field note, and later accumulated more and more margin notes during on-call work and review. It was never organized into a straight line from entry point to conclusion: the early guess about the callback pump, the misreading of jobid when there was no request, another entry point through the default protocol mask, and the later current understanding are still retained in their original order. During troubleshooting, first identify which kind of sample you have.

## 2023-06-26: Record the symptom first; do not assign a name to the incident

The initial symptom was very narrow. After a callback returned, the caller saw a result that did not match the expected text; another callback record had no request, and jobid also had no usable value. The two records had neither a call stack in common nor the values of the same object before and after entering the callback saved at the same time.

At the time, the working hypothesis was that the callback pump had performed a second wrapping. The mismatch between result in the outer log and the business-layer judgment was the only reason we could produce at the time. This reason was insufficient to determine where the rewrite occurred, but sufficient to explain why the first round started by investigating the pump.

The only actions actually possible in the first round were these: put the callback type, received result, whether a request existed, and the jobid from the log on the same line; if a request existed, also add the identifier from when the request was sent; if no request existed, record only a no-request sample. Without the value before the call, do not write "rewritten"; with only user-visible text, do not infer the underlying value backward from the text.

The simplified tree left at this point was as follows:

```text
Callback returned abnormally
├─ Has request/jobid: compare values before and after
└─ No request/jobid: first save the callback type and raw output
```

## On-call margin note: Where the path leads

During on-call work, there was no complete stack, so we could only search by public names. Older records repeatedly pointed to `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h`. Near this path, declarations containing the terms callback, result, steamuser, eresult, callbacks, request, jobid, and invalid could be seen, so it was suitable as a reading entry point.

The margin note specifically called out two things that were easy to confuse. First, names near declarations are not the same as runtime processing points; to confirm the relationship, references in the current revision still need to be followed. Second, invalid in the log is merely a recorded value and cannot by itself prove that no request exists. At that time, these notes had not been written as unified rules; the troubleshooting sheet merely circled two sticking points: identify the request first, then explain jobid.

The order of operations is therefore retained as follows: first copy the output, then check request; first confirm whether a request actually exists, then discuss jobid; if all that remains is the error text on the page, stop at that text and do not label it as an underlying conversion.

## 2024-03-05: A review that did not reach a conclusion

During the review, it was found that the old page placed callback result identity and default protocol mask in the same tree. The first step was changed to separating the two entry points, with matching to a request checked only in the second step. There were still not enough samples, so the assessment from the year 2023 was not deleted.

The result branch was changed to:

```text
callback arrives but the result is incorrect
├─ Can be matched to request/jobid
│  ├─ result differs before and after callback: save both values, check where it first changes
│  └─ result is the same before and after callback: check how the consumer interprets result
└─ Cannot be matched to request/jobid
   ├─ Sample is reproducible: record the callback type, result and original jobid value
   └─ Sample is not reproducible: stop at the output, do not infer default semantics from a single empty value
```

"check where it first changes" means continuing to examine the adjacency relationships among callback pump, direct references to handler registry and the consumer, not attributing the rewrite to one of those layers merely because a name looks similar. If EResult is the same on both sides, but only the page display differs, troubleshooting shifts to the consumer's mapping; if only the callback value is available and there is no pre-send value, troubleshooting stops at locating the object.

This round also yielded a sampling requirement: samples with a request must include the identifier at send time and the identifier at callback time; samples without a request must retain the callback type, result and original jobid value. These two kinds of samples cannot be merged under a single "no association" label. If there is only a single sporadic record with an empty field, first save the output and context, and do not write it up as a protocol rule.

## Previously used sequence (deprecated)

> When jobid is invalid, first treat it as "no request"; when result is abnormal, then check the caller's error mapping.

This passage was not deleted from the old page, because it explains why a class of samples was missed early on. [Deprecated] It treated a field's displayed value as evidence of a request relationship. Even if jobid is invalid, it may simply mean that the current record has not captured the association with the request; the three original fields request, jobid, and callback should now be retained, before determining whether a correspondence exists.

Another problem with the old sequence is that it chained two judgments into a single conclusion: first deciding "no request", then passing the anomalous result to the caller. This would exclude records that actually have a request in the very first step. When you encounter similar output, first return to the collection branch, and do not continue along this old procedure.

## After 2025: the card only added a search entry point

SK2-203 could only be cited as a navigation target after 2025-09-22. The public contract wording it retains is `JobID.Invalid`, and searches during troubleshooting and review should use that exact wording. This term resolved the search entry point issue, but did not establish the call relationship for any specific callback sample.

The public record dated 2025-09-24 notes that, in the claim that the old call retains the callback result, one callback result identity remains unconfirmed; the inputs and outputs must be kept in the rollback drill sheet. Here, "unconfirmed" only means that the samples have not all been collected yet, and must not be extrapolated into a complete call chain, nor may the old working hypothesis be treated as a verified conclusion about the implementation.

SK2-220 is another entry point for default protocol mask. It could only be cited after 2025-10-12; follow-up work had started, but was moved back to the backlog because the incident context on hand was out of date. Therefore, use it here only as a place to search for new samples: when new input is available, record what is actually returned or thrown, and when it is not, remain at the pending-samples stage rather than using old output to fill in current behavior.

## Incident troubleshooting tree: identify the object first, then decide where to stop

Symptoms may include a result that looks abnormal, a jobid that does not match the request, or an abnormal return seen through the default protocol mask entry point. Handle these three types of symptoms in separate branches.

```text
A. result or EResult looks abnormal
├─ A1. Raw request records are available
│  ├─ Both the sent value and the callback value are available
│  │  ├─ The two differ: follow direct references to find the first change
│  │  └─ The two match: switch to checking the consumer's mapping and display
│  └─ Only the callback value is available
│     └─ Stop: do not claim that result was overwritten until the sent value is obtained
└─ A2. No request records are available
   ├─ The callback type and result can be observed repeatedly
   │  └─ Save as a sample without a request, then continue examining the original jobid value
   └─ Only one occurrence or missing context
      └─ Stop: do not infer naming rules from a single invalid value or an empty field

B. jobid does not match request
├─ request is confirmed to exist: retain the three fields request, jobid, callback, and check where they are associated
├─ request is confirmed not to exist: save as a callback without a request, do not fabricate a pairing
└─ request status is unknown: return to record collection, do not proceed to attributing the result to a cause

C. An anomaly occurs at the default protocol mask entry point
├─ The returned content can be reproduced: save the entry point, input and raw return value separately
├─ An exception is thrown: save the exception text and triggering conditions, do not recast it as a callback result
└─ The incident state is stale: stop pending an additional sample, do not infer new behavior from old output
```

### Conditions for continuing the investigation

The same record must at least allow identification of the callback type, result, whether a request exists and the original jobid value, before proceeding to correlation comparisons. To determine whether the result has changed, the corresponding value from before the callback is also required; without it, only identify the object. After finding `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h`, continue checking references in the current revision, and do not treat the path as proof of implementation ownership.

If EResult is the same before and after but the page text differs, first retain both values, then examine how the consumer maps them. Do not work backward and assume that the callback pump overwrote anything just because the page displays error text. If both request and jobid are available only as log summaries, with no raw fields, the sample's correlation is still unknown.

### When you must stop

Stop if you see error text in the user interface but do not have the underlying result. Stop if you see `JobID.Invalid` but have no request context. Stop if you have only one output from default protocol mask but want to explain callback identity. If the inputs differ between the old and new incident states, also stop at the sample boundary, and do not stitch two points in time together into a single reproduction.

## Current verification guidelines

`SteamUser.LoggedOnCallback preserves the supplied EResult exactly, and callbacks without a request keep JobID.Invalid.`

This guidance answers only whether the callback result is preserved according to the supplied EResult, and what value jobid uses when there is no request. It does not replace consumer-side display checks, nor does it fold default protocol mask into the callback issue. When conflicting output is encountered, first use the three branches A, B, and C to determine whether it is an original value, an associated value, a displayed value, or a value from another entry point, and then decide whether the input and output need to be added to the rollback drill ticket.

The current record should also retain the callback type, the request relationship, and the entry-point input. If any one of these is missing, the appropriate action is to locate the gap, not infer a call relationship from field names. The compatibility check for DOC-16 is not the same incident as this one, and its contents cannot be used to replace the callback record.

## Still-open adjacent issues

default protocol mask new samples still have not all been collected. We need to see what the public entry point actually returns, whether it throws an exception, and whether the input is the same as in the old case; "entry-point support" must not be expanded into a guarantee for all connection states.

Another unresolved item is the consumption order in the handler registry. The current material is sufficient only to list it as a checkpoint after result preservation; it is not enough to assert that a particular handler rewrote the text seen by users. If a consumer-side mapping is found later, its correspondence with the original EResult should be added, rather than rewriting the current guidance on this page.

## Meeting margin notes

> First find the callback's original result; do not look at the error sentence on the page first. Put samples with no request aside, and compare them only once they can be reproduced.

This sentence can still guide the on-site investigation, but it provides no invocation command and does not assume that any particular logging system necessarily exists. This is consistent with the review tree from the year 2024; as for whether the specific samples are comparable, the input, output, and request records remain the basis for judgment.

## Retained old examples

### Old example A: Only one callback log

The input contains only a callback name and a piece of result text, with no request, jobid, or pre-send record. The old practice would label it "request failed." This label is obsolete; it can now only be recorded as a result anomaly, pending a complete sample from the same entry point. It cannot prove that callback pump performed wrapping.

### Old example B: Same result but different page display

Old records described the difference in page text as a rewritten callback result. Later review found that the record lacked consumer-side mapping information, so a display-layer transformation could not be ruled out. Therefore, this old example is retained as a counterexample: once the results have been compared and found to be the same, check the consumer side rather than continuing to speculate along the callback pump.

### Old example C: Outdated output from default protocol mask

A sample containing only an output summary was previously kept, but the input conditions were not fully documented. It cannot be used to confirm the current entry point's behavior, and it is attached here to preserve the reason the earlier investigation was not closed out. A new sample must at least include the entry point, input, and raw response together; if only an outdated summary is available, stop because the samples are insufficient.

### Old example D: No request and invalid were written up as the same thing

Early records placed the description of a missing request alongside the invalid field, making it easy for later readers to mistake juxtaposition for causation. These two items must now be recorded separately: whether a request exists is a fact about the association, while jobid is a field value in the record. Continue comparing only when both can be confirmed from the same context.

Ultimately, the actual entry point for reading remains `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h`; the navigable cards are SK2-203, SK2-220. If the entry point cannot provide the same comparable record, leave the unknowns unresolved, and do not use the compatibility-check content from the adjacent documents DOC-16 to fill in the callback details on this page.

This requirement explains why subscription changes cannot be checked by looking only at a static registration declaration: callback execution uses an immutable snapshot, a callback can dispose of another subscription, and registration and unregistration must remain safe at the same time. # Exception Context and List Refresh Proposal

The earlier draft put the two issues on the same track because the old investigation notes pointed to `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h` based on the issue names and call names. That version also treated the "existing h module" as a sufficient starting point for interface checks. That judgment is retained here as the working premise at the time; following the review, it can no longer be used to infer runtime ownership.

What we can directly confirm at the frozen revision is still limited to local declarations. line 40 is `namespace internal {`, line 41 is `class AnyMetadata;`, line 46 is `struct TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto {`, and line 59 is `class CBilling_Address;`, followed further down by `CBilling_AddressDefaultTypeInternal`, `CCDDBAppDetailCommon`, and the corresponding `DefaultTypeInternal` declarations. These show that the file can serve as an index for reading the code and cross-checking historical behavior, but do not by themselves establish that `exception context` or `server-list freshness` is carried out here.

The proposed approach therefore switches to two parallel verification tracks.

* **Continue tracing from the declarations.** First retain the local locations in the header, then use the known names to look for direct references. This keeps the scope narrow and makes it easy to add the results back to the old notes. The trade-off is that even if the references match, they establish only object relationships; declarations alone cannot prove how exception state or server-list freshness changes.
* **Work from usage scenarios.** Do not treat the debug entry point as representative. Record the pre-call state, the call action, and the raw result after the call completes. This track is slower, but separates interface review from the changes users actually see. If we end up with only declarations and names, with no before-and-after state, the conclusion stops at "entry point unconfirmed."

The test for `exception context` follows the local requirements in SK2-207: start the reproduction from the pre-call state, then check whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. Here, record as "changes" only the return contents, content attached to exceptions, or state differences that are actually visible. Do not assume that new fields will necessarily be added, and do not treat filenames appearing in a stack trace as interface behavior. First retain the raw output from one success path and one exception path. If all the two runs show is the same exception type, with no other visible differences, record that result; do not conclude from it that the context has been cleared or retained.

For `server-list freshness`, use the entry point specified by SK2-224: have it go through users' routine calls rather than the debug entry point, and retain the return value or raw diagnostics. This choice avoids using the debug path as evidence for routine calls. Record both the list results used by the call and the diagnostic text obtained at the time; if a routine call has no return value that can be retained, first record the gap rather than inventing another successful sample. The earlier draft's statement that "the processed return value should be stable" is only a hypothesis to verify, not an expected test result.

The two tracks have not been collapsed into a single implementation decision, either. If the declaration track finds clear direct references first, it can narrow the search scope for the second track; it cannot replace that track. If a usage scenario shows a change, still return to the corresponding local declarations to check the names and locations. Conversely, if the header yields only a list of objects, the proposal does not expand to interface changes; it retains only the review record and unresolved questions.

Keep the withdrawal criteria narrow: if the review cannot distinguish changes in `exception context` by comparing before and after a call, or `server-list freshness` has no return value or raw diagnostics to retain from routine calls, withdraw the unified assessment of the two behaviors; retain the header navigation references and the gaps for each. If direct references show that the two actually use different objects, also withdraw the old "shared entry point" assumption; do not combine them just to reach a single review conclusion. We do not have the material in this round to decide whether to change the public interface or remove the old entry point.

# Symmetric Decryption and Trading Retirement Troubleshooting Tree

This old record was used as an entry point for investigating exceptions throughout the wrap-up of 3.0.0-alpha.3, for a simple reason: `symmetric wire decryption` and `legacy trading removal` often appeared together in search results. This juxtaposition came from troubleshooting habits at the time, not from a confirmed causal relationship. During the later follow-up review, the most important thing to preserve turned out to be this distinction: one name describes the failure boundary around wire data decryption, while the other describes whether legacy trading functionality can still be reached from a particular call site.

The old entry point leads to `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/crypto.h`. The repository index classifies it as an existing h module, making declarations and references suitable starting points for reviewing historical behavior. Earlier notes made "this file can be found by searching for the issue name" sound almost as though the implementation had been located; that wording is no longer accurate enough, but it has not been deleted because some people still use this file as their starting point for review. A file path can narrow the reading scope, but it cannot replace call relationships, much less establish on its own which exception originated there.

## Start by Separating the Names Based on the Incident

If the reported symptom is that encrypted wire data cannot be processed further, or that processing stops with an exception near network frame handling, do not label it legacy right away. First preserve three things: the layer containing the input, where the key is obtained, and whether the exception occurs before or after decryption. If any of these three is missing, subsequent search hits for `crypto.h`, crypto, key, or encrypted are only starting points for reading.

The old record contains a sequence that can easily lead to incorrect action: first search for crypto, then adjust whichever declarations happen to turn up, and finally rerun the triggering path. This recovery procedure left no comparable boundary. Changes to declarations can obscure the original symptoms; running the failed input through again as ordinary plaintext does not prove that wire decryption has recovered either. For incidents like this, therefore, do not list changing header files, changing names, or repackaging the input as recovery methods. Only by preserving the original boundary first can the next result be compared at the same point.

Another type of incident is that legacy trading functionality remains accessible somewhere. There is no need to collect wire data first, nor should decryption declarations be traced first. What needs to be checked is the version the caller actually uses, the entry point it uses, and the result it currently gets. Only when these three line up can the incident be recorded as an issue at the removal boundary. Knowing only the old name does not establish that the entry point still exists; knowing only that one entry point was deleted does not establish that no other call paths exist.

The early investigation put both tracks in the same passage so that on-call staff would need one fewer search window, not so that the two tracks could share evidence. This convention still applies: when both names appear in the same incident, establish two tracks first, then decide whether to combine the narrative. The wire track focuses on the input boundary, key source, and exception location; the trading track focuses on the caller version, entry point, and result. When one side lacks material, do not fill the gap with material already found on the other side.

```text
Names seen in the incident
├─ symmetric wire decryption
│  ├─ Record the layer containing the input
│  ├─ Record where the key is obtained
│  └─ Record whether the exception occurs before or after decryption
│     └─ Then trace back through references to crypto.h
└─ legacy trading removal
   ├─ Confirm the caller's actual version
   ├─ Confirm the entry point that remains accessible
   └─ Record the current result
      └─ Do not merge into the wire decryption track
```

Neither endpoint in the diagram means "fix complete". They are simply the stopping points used in the old record. Without confirmed references, the decryption branch stops at the file and name; without a confirmed caller, entry point, and result, the trading branch stops at the old name. This may seem conservative, but it prevents a single search hit from being expanded into a release judgment.

## Past Incidents on the wire Branch

When starting from wire symptoms, first distinguish whether the exception occurs before or after decryption. The former at least indicates that the incident has not yet passed the decryption step; the latter indicates that the exception context needs to be examined alongside the key already obtained and the ciphertext boundary. Here, "before" and "after" locate the issue in the troubleshooting sequence; they are not assertions about a specific implementation file. The existing record contains no function names, full call stacks, or reproducible commands, so a more detailed execution chain must not be filled in.

If the only stack available is near the network-handling layer, still preserve the wire boundary and key source first, then look for references. The network-handling layer alone is not enough to distinguish declarations, implementations, and callers; directly attributing such a stack to `crypto.h` was an overreach in the old record. If tracing references back does not lead to a definite usage site, the incident should be recorded as "call site not confirmed", not "crypto implementation located".

If the decryption call can already be identified, the recording method remains the same: list where the key is obtained, the wire boundary, and the exception point side by side. Do not leave only the four Chinese characters for "decryption failed". That kind of summary cannot distinguish whether the key source is already known, whether the input boundary is complete, or whether the exception really occurred during decryption. The old page did not specify which module should provide this material; it only required that the three items not be conflated into one vague crypto issue.

Failures that appeared only after fragmentation or reconnection were once noted beside the wire branch as conditions worth preserving. They are not confirmed causes, nor do they justify skipping the recording of the input boundary and exception location. In particular, when there is only one failure after reconnection and no repeat record from the same call site, it should not be described as a repeatable decryption regression. The old on-call addendum serves only as a reminder: timing differences like these make the "search crypto first" approach more likely to mislead.

There is another incomplete type of incident: the issue name contains symmetric or encrypted, but neither the key source nor the exception context is available. In this case, the file path can still be used to start reading, but that is where the investigation should stop. Continuing to infer a specific algorithm, implementation ownership, or corrective action from the name is beyond what this record supports. Follow-up review should return to the reference relationships in the same repository revision, rather than backfilling conclusions based on similar names found in later searches.

## The trading Branch Did Not Borrow Decryption Evidence

The checking sequence for `legacy trading removal` differs from that of the wire branch. First ask which version the caller actually depends on; while the version is unclear, whether the entry point still exists has no explanatory value. Once the version is confirmed, find the entry point. If the entry point is clear but the result is not recorded, removal should not be described as having taken effect or not having taken effect either. This sequence was designed for remaining legacy callers, not as a general release checklist.

The removal in the old title can easily suggest that all related calls in the repository have already been removed. The available material supports treating it only as a starting point for a regression investigation pending verification: a caller still using the functionality must be found, and its actual version, entry point, and current result must be confirmed. This pending item has still not been fleshed out with a concrete example on this page, so "no caller can be found" and "no caller exists" must not be treated as the same statement.

If an incident proves only that an old trading name appeared, simply record the name. If an incident proves only that one entry point was deleted, keep that as a local change as well, without extrapolating to other entry points. Inserting these remnants into the wire decryption timeline would create the false impression that the decryption exceptions already have a shared root cause. The two kinds of material must remain separate until call relationships within the same revision can actually connect them.

In an early draft, "the trading entry point is still being called" was written as though it were an observed fact. The later review did not supply the actual caller, version, or result, so this statement should be read as a working hypothesis, not as a current assessment. It is retained to explain why removal was included among the troubleshooting entry points at the time; it should not be used as a basis for planning any changes to wire decryption.

## Limitations When Tracing Back from the File Entry Point

`Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/crypto.h` is the only explicitly retained code navigation point on this page. It can help with reading existing declarations and checking the names used in the old investigation. On its own, it cannot answer "who calls this", "whether decryption is implemented here", or "whether this exception was triggered by this code". The version tag used by the old record is `v_prev`, so relationships derived from the file must be based on references in that version; neighboring code seen during the current review cannot simply be substituted into the old incident.

The tracing process can be broken into very small steps. First inspect the declarations in that revision; then see which locations reference those declarations; only then match definite usage sites to the input boundary or legacy trading entry point in the incident. If any step yields no definite location, return to the material from the previous step rather than continuing to fill in a call chain based on names. This sequence does not guarantee that the root cause will be found, but it keeps "the file was mentioned" and "the call was confirmed" as two distinct states.

Someone once proposed treating `crypto.h` as the central patch point for all encryption exceptions. That recommendation no longer applies. It ignored the facts preserved here: the file is an h module, the old investigation pointed to it from issue names and call names, and the actual relationships still have to be checked through references. This old recommendation is retained to prevent the next review from once again treating a header file path as the scope of changes.

## Incident Branches and Stopping Points

1. **Only the `symmetric wire decryption` name is available, with no stack.** Record the name and the context in which it was seen, and add whatever is already available about the input layer, key source, and exception location; if the caller cannot yet be identified, stop at the file entry point.

2. **A stack is available, but it only reaches the vicinity of network handling.** Preserve the wire boundary and whether the exception is before or after decryption, then trace references back. If the stack does not clearly identify a decryption call, do not modify declarations or state that the network-handling layer owns the implementation.

3. **There is a definite decryption call, but the incident lacks the key source or input boundary.** Preserve the known exception point and continue to mark the missing items as missing. "The decryption call has been reached" cannot substitute for the other two items.

4. **Only the `legacy trading removal` name is available.** Check the caller version and entry point; if the two cannot be matched, the name remains only a starting point, and no judgment is made on whether removal is complete.

5. **There are clues to a legacy trading call.** Record the version, entry point, and result separately. If the result is missing, retain it as an incomplete check rather than putting it into the recovery record for decryption exceptions.

6. **Both names appear in the same incident.** Preserve the two tracks separately. Discuss whether a shared explanation is needed only when the call relationships on both sides can be verified within the same revision; the existing record has not met this condition.

These branches are the reading sequence left by the old on-call page, not new release gate rules. Their value is in telling later readers which materials should not be mixed together. In particular, the three weak clues "finding the file in a search", "seeing the old name", and "having a network-layer stack" cannot independently establish that the implementation has been located or removal is complete.

## Corrections from This Review

The review added the distinction between the file entry point and actual calls, and separated the evidence requirements for the two names. It did not add specific functions, implementation files, commands, complete logs, or successful results, because the material preserved on this page does not contain them. Missing does not mean nonexistent; it only means that this old record cannot replace a recheck of the revision and caller.

DOC-21 can serve as an adjacent starting point for compatibility checks, but it does not provide the stacks, references, or caller evidence missing from this page. When starting there, still follow the two tracks here, rather than combining the two pages into a single conclusion.

Questions that remain from the incident:

- Which specific caller originally pointed `symmetric wire decryption` to this file?
- Are the actual entry point and version of `legacy trading removal` related to the caller above?
- In the old revision, where are the declarations, usage sites, and exception boundaries respectively?

Until corresponding code or incident excerpts are available for these questions, this record preserves only the troubleshooting starting point, branches, and stopping points.

# Crypto Interface and CM List Compatibility Notes

The initial draft tracked crypto API retirement and legacy CM-list retirement separately; that decision stands. Both appear to involve "old entry points that may still be in use," but the checks target different things: the crypto item needs to be traced to callers still using the old crypto interface; the CM-list item needs to be traced to the old list usage pattern associated with the anomaly. Combining them would let a single failure to reproduce output obscure a usage pattern in the other item that has not yet been pinpointed.

Start migration records with the caller, not a bulk name replacement. For each check, first record the caller's actual version, entry point, and result at the time. Only discuss changing that caller once those three line up. `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h` remains a reference for revisiting old names and adjacent declarations; it helps identify historical items but cannot replace caller records.

The initial draft made "the name can be found near the declaration" sound too much like a completion criterion. This has been corrected to a navigation clue. Whether migration is complete still depends on whether the caller has been checked and whether the post-switch result is retained in the same record.

```text
Before migration
Caller ──> Old crypto interface
Caller ──> Old CM-list usage pattern

During verification
Caller ──> Version / Entry point / Result at the time
                     │
                     ├──> Switch can be recorded
                     └──> Unconfirmed: leave unchanged

When rollback is needed
Affected caller ──> Pre-migration entry point
```

## crypto item

SK2-209 began with an inability to consistently reproduce the output from crypto API retirement. Do not treat a single failure to reproduce it as meaning the old interface is no longer reachable, or use it to mark the retirement as complete. First find the callers still using that old interface, then record the actual version, entry point, and current result together; if only the issue name is known and the entry point has not been located, the status remains unconfirmed.

After review, one point in this item remains unconfirmed, so SK2-209 is not marked complete. Subsequent records should fill in that one caller or usage location, rather than repeat broad checks without a corresponding entry point. If that caller does switch later, the record must retain both the pre-switch entry point and the post-switch result, so that "not consistently reproduced" can be distinguished from "the entry point is no longer in use."

## CM-list item

SK2-226 points to an anomaly in a specific usage pattern of legacy CM-list; it does not mean that all session-related usage can be handled under the same conclusion. When checking, first record what purpose the old list serves for that caller, then confirm whether it is still being used as a session source. Do not proceed with a switch if an anomaly is known but the specific usage pattern is not.

The CM-list item does not reuse results from the crypto item. Even if a caller has been found on the crypto side, that does not establish that the old list usage pattern can be replaced; conversely, an anomaly in one old list usage pattern does not imply that the old crypto interface is still producing output. The two items have separate records so that a later rollback affects only one caller or one usage pattern.

## Switching and Rollback

For each caller slated for a change, keep only four fields: caller, pre-migration entry point, the retirement item to be addressed in that change, and rollback target. The item to be addressed must be written as either crypto API retirement or legacy CM-list retirement; if both come up together, split them into two records. This prevents an anomaly in CM-list from being recorded as a crypto issue during rollback.

If any fields are still blank before the switch, stay on the original entry point; do not fill in results based on adjacent declarations in the header file. If the result cannot be confirmed after the change, roll the affected caller back to the pre-migration entry point and mark it as a compatibility exception; do not make the old crypto interface and old CM-list usage pattern default paths again.

| Check | What must be recorded before the change | Rollback scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| crypto API retirement | Caller version, old interface entry point, current result | That caller |
| legacy CM-list retirement | Specific old list usage pattern, session source assessment | That usage pattern |

DOC-22 records independent validation of fragmented stream reads, which is not combined with these two retirement checks. To track the unconfirmed crypto item, see SK2-209; to fill in the old list usage pattern, see SK2-226.

# Encoded Null Termination Decision Record

This record was originally for a compatibility investigation involving alpha.3. The issue name contained encoded, null, and termination, so attention quickly shifted to the generated message file. The initial draft pushed this direction too far, as if the termination condition could be settled from the declarations alone; in practice, all that remained was a search location that could be revisited, with no call record sufficient to explain read/write behavior.

`Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steammessages_base.pb.h` remains in place. The `namespace internal {` at the start of the file, the subsequent `class AnyMetadata;`, and `struct TableStruct_steammessages_5fbase_2eproto {` can return the investigation to the same set of message declarations. `class CBilling_Address;` and the adjacent default-type declaration serve the same purpose: they identify objects within the generated unit, not which object owns the termination bytes.

The draft carefully compared two paths. The first treated the header file as the requirements boundary: write compatibility conventions around the table structure and message classes first, then require callers to handle nulls accordingly. Its advantages were a clear file and a visible stopping point for the discussion. The cost was not fully spelled out at the time: a declaration location can indicate only names and structural adjacency; it cannot show that a particular object is responsible for writing, appending, or consuming the termination content.

The second was to reduce the header to a verification entry point. First locate the actual call, then inspect the content passed in, what is visible at the receiving end, and the failure symptoms; defer judgment on the termination condition until after that evidence. The draft chose the second path, but one part now looks too optimistic: finding a single call does not mean that all message paths are covered. At the time, this was only a working assumption and should not be read as a complete rule.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Declaration review
    Declaration review --> Call to be added
    Call to be added --> Termination condition TBD
```

# Encrypted Manifest Parsing Troubleshooting Tree

When you encounter a discrepancy in encrypted manifest parsing results, do not immediately attribute the problem to the manifest contents or decryption order. Existing legacy records carry only the issue name and call name to `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h`; first confirm what references actually surround this path in that revision, then decide whether to continue tracing toward the parsing side.

First collect an input description that can be checked: where the input comes from, when it is marked encrypted, and whether the discrepancy occurs before or after reading. Without a concrete input, only record the missing items; make no implementation changes.

```text
Result discrepancy
├─ Has a concrete input
│  ├─ Path check finds a match: retain the matching location, then inspect adjacent references
│  └─ Path check finds no match: retain the no-match record, stop guessing about the association
└─ No concrete input
   └─ Do not proceed to implementation; add the input source and reproduction conditions
```

When checking the path, use the repository's own path-checking method, and leave one match record and one no-match record. A match does not mean `steamtypes.h` is the implementation location; it only shows that the old record still points here as the starting point for reading. If the reference check does not connect the input, parsing, and this path, stop at that conclusion; do not use the filename to complete the relationship.
