# Encrypted Manifest Parsing Troubleshooting Tree

When a difference in results is reported for encrypted manifest parsing, the three things most easily conflated during troubleshooting are: whether a concrete input is available, whether the account supplied by the caller can be obtained in the current environment, and whether the old troubleshooting entry point still leads to readable nearby source code. Any of them can halt troubleshooting, but they are not the same kind of halt.

The earliest recorded entry point is still `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h`. The old records located this entry point using the issue name and call name, so this is a suitable place to start looking back; do not treat the manifest contents, the decryption operation, and the parsing result as an established sequence based on this filename alone. First confirm the reference in the current revision, then attach this input or the missing information near that reference.

Follow the tree below this time. The "Stop" in the tree does not mean closing the issue, but pausing a technical judgment that lacks the prerequisites to proceed.

```text
encrypted manifest parsing result differences
|
+-- Is a concrete input available?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Record what is missing about the input: its source, the basis for labeling it encrypted, where the difference appears
|   |   +-- Use repository path checks to retain one match and one no-match result
|   |   `-- Stop implementation and attribution; wait for input that can be verified
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Can the account be used in the current environment?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No
|       |   |   `-- Record the permissions blocker; do not record an access failure as a parsing failure
|       |   |
|       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |
|       |       +-- Can path checks connect the old entry point to the relevant references?
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   +-- No
|       |       |   |   `-- Keep the no-match record, return to the input description to check naming and source
|       |       |   |
|       |       |   `-- Yes
|       |       |       `-- Record the reference locations, input conditions, and observed differences, then decide whether implementation-level verification is needed
|       |       |
|       `-- After any prerequisite changes, start again from the top of the tree
|
`-- Do not substitute card status for a technical conclusion
```

## Clarify the Input First

A "concrete input" here must at least answer three specific questions: which caller or storage location it came from; why it is considered encrypted; whether the difference was seen while obtaining the content, when entering parsing, or when using the results after parsing. Without this information, a "difference in results" should not be recorded as a fault in a particular field, function, or piece of decryption logic.

The input description does not need to reproduce the entire contents. If the content is restricted, you can still leave a way to identify it without revealing the content itself, such as the source name, provider, whether it can be obtained again, and the stage at which the difference was observed. The point is to ensure that whoever checks next knows they are comparing the same item, rather than two manifests with similar names.

If the provider can only say "there is a problem with the encrypted manifest" without a sample, just record that statement as the reported symptom. Do not infer from it that every encrypted manifest will fail, or add exception messages that have never appeared to the record. What can be done at this point is a path check, not verification of parsing behavior.

## Path Checks

When using `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/steamtypes.h` as the starting point for reading, use the repository's existing path-checking method and leave two types of results:

- One match record: state the path or reference location the check reached, and its direct relationship to this input description;
- One no-match record: state which term or relationship was checked, and where it was not found, without rewriting "no results" as "the implementation does not exist".

These two records serve different purposes. The match record gives subsequent readers an anchor they can return to; the no-match record keeps the next person on call from continuing to guess using names that have already been tried. Neither is equivalent to a reproduction result.

The old records retained this h file because it provided an entry point for reading the code and checking historical behavior at the time. It does not automatically establish where this difference belongs. If the path check only finds objects with the same name, comments, or nonadjacent declarations, write "there is a text match, but it has not yet been connected to the input path", and do not elevate it to a conclusion about parsing. Conversely, if the check finds no match, do not jump straight to guessing about filename decryption ordering; DOC-26 records another entry point for compatibility checks, and similar names cannot replace the input and references required on this page.

## Permissions Branch

SK2-213 was moved to Blocked during one round of handling, because the account supplied by the caller did not have permission in that environment. This only shows that the environment could not obtain or view the required content using the method supplied at the time. It does not prove that parsing succeeded, nor does it prove that parsing failed.

When the account is unusable, record the environment and access result, then stop at the permissions branch. Do not treat content that was never obtained as an empty manifest to get around the blocker, and do not include subsequent empty results after access was denied in the parsing assessment. If a usable account or environment is provided later, start again from "Is a concrete input available", because the input's source and availability may both have changed.

Do not proceed directly to implementation changes after permissions are restored either. First check whether the input obtained after access was restored is the same one described earlier; if the input's identity is still unclear, the problem has merely changed from "no access" to "the object obtained cannot be confirmed". Keep these two types of records separate.

## Minimal Verification Once Input Is Available

When the input, account, and path references are all available, the record should cover only what was observed this time:

1. Where the input was obtained, and where its encrypted label came from;
2. Where the path check found a match, or the fact that it could not connect to the relevant references;
3. The stage at which the difference was first seen;
4. Whether the same input can be obtained again in the current environment;
5. Whether parsing-level verification was actually performed this time.

The fifth item is important. A path match and a usable account do not automatically mean that parsing has been verified. If only the first four items have been completed, describe the work as "the prerequisites are in place, but implementation-level verification has not yet begun". Do not cover this gap with a vague "already checked".

If the difference appears before the content is obtained, stop extending the investigation into parsing; first return to the input source and permission conditions. If the content can be obtained and the references can be connected, but the difference is only seen where the results are used after parsing, record that observation location, rather than retroactively recording it as a failure of the parsing process. Only continue examining the code near the references when actual observations place the difference in the parsing stage.

## Where Work Previously Stopped

The first draft of this page listed "missing concrete input" as the primary gap, and there was not enough material at the time to treat the old path entry point as identifying the responsible implementation. That judgment still stands: the file entry point can be used to start reading, but it cannot replace the input.

The later blocker record for SK2-213 added an independent condition: the caller's account lacked access in the environment at the time. This condition explains why no more material could be obtained during troubleshooting, but it did not eliminate the original input gap. Combining the permission issue and the missing input into "the environment is wrong" hides two different recovery paths: one is to complete the input description, and the other is to restore usable access.

A later note on the same card requested that it not be closed yet, because one aspect of encrypted manifest parsing remained unconfirmed and concrete input was missing, so implementation would not begin for now. Here, "implementation would not begin for now" should be taken literally: do not make code changes without input, rather than treating it as confirmation that the existing implementation needs no verification.

The last retained status action was a move from Blocked back to To Do, because the original owner was away that week and the card should not continue occupying an in-progress slot. This was a scheduling change, not a signal of technical recovery. After the card returns to the backlog, the input, permissions, and references branches on this page must still be checked again, and the status change should not be taken to mean that a sample has been supplied, the account has been restored, or the parsing relationships have been clarified.

## Recovery Actions to Avoid

- Do not treat a failure result following denied access as a failure sample for encrypted manifest parsing.
- Do not make changes directly at `steamtypes.h` just because the old records point there; first locate references related to this input.
- Do not compare different manifests by name without concrete input, or use records on neighboring topics to fill the gaps on this page.
- Do not omit the no-match record after "a path match was found". Without a no-match record, it is difficult to tell next time which names, relationships, or directions have already been tried.
- Do not delete the permissions record just because SK2-213 moved from blocked back to the backlog. It describes the environment limitation at the time, and later verification may encounter the same limitation.

These actions are tempting because they appear to keep the card moving, but they add no verifiable input or reference relationships. Preserving the stopping point is more useful than assigning a cause without evidence.

## What to Leave in the Handoff

Handoff information should stay close to the branch taken this time, rather than being written as an abstract conclusion. You can add a short section in the following order:

```text
Input: provided / not provided; source: ……
Access: available / unavailable; account result in the environment: ……
Path: match location: ……; no-match check: ……
Difference: location where first seen: ……
Stopped at: obtain input / handle permissions / recheck references / begin implementation-level verification
```

Blank fields may be left blank, but do not fill them with guesses. If all that is known is that the account lacks access, record only the permissions branch; if only the path checks have been completed, record only the match and no-match results. This lets the next person see whether the missing prerequisite is material, access conditions, or code relationships.

## Still to Be Confirmed

There is currently no concrete input that can be archived on this page, and the old path entry point has not been connected to the parsing call for any particular input. The next time material becomes available, prioritize completing the input description and the two path-check records; if the environment continues to reject the caller's account, retain that blocker first and do not begin implementation. SK2-213 can serve as the issue entry point, but the card's status does not replace the branch judgments here.

versions.body:
# Single-Entry ZIP Integrity Proposal

The interface review for 3.0.0-alpha.3 began with a very narrow assumption: when the input contains only one ZIP entry, integrity issues could be addressed entirely in ZIP handling. The earlier draft therefore treated `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/zip.h` as the primary place to make the change, with a local adjustment planned around single-entry ZIP integrity.

## Options Considered at the Time

One option was to restrict the input shape in ZIP handling. Parsing would stop if more than one entry was found, so downstream callers would receive only single-entry results. The advantages were a centralized rule and an easy-to-find entry point. The cost was that existing callers that accepted multi-entry archives would fail earlier, potentially changing both where the error occurred and how it was returned.

Another option was to leave the handler unchanged and check the entry count only in callers that consume the result. This would be more permissive toward existing inputs, but the same check would be spread across multiple call sites. A missed check could still produce a result that "looks successful but has incomplete contents." The review did not leave enough material to confirm the number of callers, nor did it establish which failure outcomes were already part of the public interface.

The earlier draft favored the first option and made "accept only one entry" the main criterion for single-entry ZIP integrity. That judgment is retained here, but subsequently could no longer be treated directly as an interface guarantee: a single entry establishes only the archive's shape and cannot replace verification of the content read result.

## Rollback Conditions and Boundaries

If experiments show that existing callers depend on multi-entry input, or that failing at the entry point changes the identity of an existing result, the direct restriction on `zip.h` should be withdrawn. Observation should continue before advancing the local proposal to the interface layer. If the only need is to record the input shape, the entry count and read completion status can be recorded first, followed by a decision on whether failure handling belongs in the handler or the caller.

This page covers only the choice of approach for ZIP handling. The actual caller versions, entry points, and results have not yet been established in this draft; these remain to be verified, not filled in with assumptions.

## Interface Shape Confirmed by the Header

The frozen `zip.h` contains very little: it includes `steam/steamtypes.h`, declares `CZip`, and exposes only the static `Inflate(const uint8 *pCompressed, uint32 cubCompressed, uint8 *pDecompressed, uint32 cubDecompressed)` publicly. This confirms that the caller supplies the compressed input, compressed length, destination buffer, and destination length together; the header provides no entry enumeration, archive directory, or multi-entry policy.

The earlier draft's proposal to "limit the entry count here" therefore remains an option to test, not existing behavior that can be inferred from this declaration. If experimentation continues, evidence of the entry shape and the buffer result from `Inflate` should be saved separately. The rollback conditions above should then be used to decide whether the restriction still belongs at this layer.

# Caller Integration Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

This records a very specific incident in adj-steamkit2: the same client / extension call target reported different current revisions at two points in time. When first observed, the state on the page did not match the state the caller actually received. Calls could still proceed using real samples, so it wasn't written up at the time as the entire project being unavailable; but integration feedback could no longer be explained directly using the page's last value.

## Incident Excerpts

- First observed: the compatibility seam differed from the old record.
- Initial action: preserved the original input and the version of `docs/adj-steamkit2/incidents/SteamKit2-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md` at the time, and stopped retrying.
- Incident side note: fixture replay was kept to one side, but there wasn't yet enough input and output to count as evidence of recovery.
- Observed result: the user path could later be restored, and the consumer contract could be reconstructed, but why the regression lane changed was still unknown.

At the time, the impact could only be recorded at the caller integration level. Compatibility assessments for real client and extension samples were affected. Integration feedback needed to be checked against the saved object state and entry-point records, not just the page's current value. There was no material showing the same change in adjacent projects, so those projects were not included in the impact scope.

The exact times of the two observations weren't recorded. The missing field is left blank here:

```text
Missing timestamps: ____
```

This blank indicates missing information from the incident; neither the export file's timestamp nor the last line of green output is treated as the anomaly's start time. Being able to continue along the recovery path does not mean the reason the two current revisions diverged is already known.

## What Was Left Open at the Time

compatibility seam, wire framing, and handler registry were only possible places to look next at the time. They weren't tied to an input, output, or call record, so they cannot be cited as causes in this version of the record. Speculation about adjacent services was also left out.

Preserving the original entry point, original input, and later recovery result is meant to keep these things from overwriting one another: the first inconsistency was the observed incident, recovery was a later action, and the uncertainty about the regression lane remains an unresolved issue.

# Postmortem on the Dual-State Anomaly in Caller Integration Testing

The earliest recorded problem was not a simple call failure, but the same client / extension call object showing different current revision values at two points in time. The caller still had real samples to run, and the page could still be opened; the problem was that the value last displayed on the page, the value in the old records, and the value obtained during integration testing could not simply be combined into a single explanation. This discrepancy was enough to lead to an incorrect version assessment in the integration feedback, but was not enough on its own to identify which change had caused it.

This postmortem keeps the original records, the later recovery results, and the unconfirmed causes separate. The original records answer "what was observed at the time", the recovery results answer "which user path worked again later", and the unconfirmed items preserve the point that "there is still no evidence of what happened between the two states". These are not the same layer of evidence, and the earlier anomaly cannot be erased just because green output appeared at the end.

## What Was First Recorded During Testing

The first note recorded only a fairly narrow observation: the real call samples generated by client and extension did not match the current revision shown on the page. That version did not include a reliable start time, nor did it extend the scope of the anomaly to all callers. The entry point that could be preserved was:

`docs/adj-steamkit2/incidents/SteamKit2-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md`

This path belongs to SteamKit2 · Client Integration's incident-export. It can lead people back to the exported records and attachments from that time, but the path itself cannot show which action produced the two revision values. The original records need to be viewed alongside the recovery page, and you cannot just open the page to see the post-recovery value.

There was also an incomplete record from the session:

```text
Missing timestamp: ____
```

The blank has been left as is. No precise timestamp was found that could fill it, so the export time, page refresh time, or handoff time is not used to infer the start of the anomaly. The impact window can only be documented as the observed period from when the inconsistency was noticed to when the caller's path recovered, and a longer period of production impact cannot be inferred from when the file appeared.

The actions taken at the time were to first save the original input and entry-point version, then stop retrying. This was not intended to prove that the entry point had changed, but to prevent the next result from overwriting the first observation. Later, the user path could be restored, and the recovery result was appended alongside the original incident; this result shows that the path was usable again, not that the two states had stabilized or that the cause had been found.

## Reviewing Events in the Order Observed

| Order | What was seen at the time | Subsequent action | What this step still did not establish |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+00 | The current revision corresponding to the caller sample did not match the old record | Preserved the original record, original input, and entry-point version | Did not prove that the entry point had just changed at that moment |
| T+07 | The same object produced another current revision at another point in time | Retained both results side by side | Did not prove that either result was necessarily an erroneous value |
| T+18 | During comparison, callback pump was seen first, and attention then shifted to handler registry | Narrowed the scope of the check without turning the clue into a causal attribution | Did not prove that either of these locations changed the object's state |
| T+31 | The user path was restored, and the consumer contract could be realigned | Appended the recovery result while retaining the failure window | Did not prove that the recovery action fixed the root cause |
| Subsequent review | Could only retrace the current entry point to portions that had already been seen | Stopped elaborating on the unreproduced branch | Did not prove that neighboring projects were involved in the change |

This timeline uses relative order in the incident, not calendar time. The source material supports only two mutually contradictory observations, subsequent partial review, and path recovery; it cannot rewrite any of those ordering points as absolute dates. The two terms in T+18 likewise only indicate the directions checked at the time: the local state of callback pump did not explain the anomaly, and there was also not enough of a handler registry fragment to attribute the root cause to it.

"Another point in time" likewise cannot be collapsed into a single, unique version-switch moment. When the second current revision appeared, the incident record did not say who changed the object, whether the entry point had been replaced, or whether the value on the page had already refreshed. Retaining the ordering is closer to the actual record than adding a seemingly precise time with no source.

## Impact boundary

Initially, it was easy to describe the problem as SteamKit2 · Client Integration being entirely unavailable. The remaining evidence did not support that scope. What can be established is that the object state the caller uses to determine the compatibility boundary is unstable; therefore, a single integration report cannot directly answer which current revision is in effect, nor can the final page value alone determine which state the client or extension sample corresponds to.

This affects the assessment during integration debugging, but it does not mean that every caller failed. No record shows that all clients simultaneously received incorrect results, nor does any record show that all extensions exhibited two states. Actual invocation samples were indeed affected; whether callers outside the sample were affected in the same way was not confirmed in the incident record. Here, we did not expand "one object was inconsistent" into "the entire project was interrupted."

Adjacent projects were not included either. Although Resources · Compatibility Catalog, Samples · Quality Signal Board, and LICENSE · Release Automation are in the same workspace, there is no evidence in this incident showing that their states contributed to this discrepancy. Their names cannot stand in for call samples, the current revision, or request context. Including them in the scope of impact would instead lead readers to believe that a cross-project comparison had already been completed.

The impact also has a boundary in time. When the two values were first observed, the integration-testing assessment was already blocked; after the path was restored, the user could proceed, but the earlier failure window still existed. The green result after recovery cannot recast that window as "never anomalous", nor can it show that the next call of the same kind will necessarily return the same value. This page therefore retains all three things: the originals showing the inconsistency, the recovery record for the usable path, and the still-unconfirmed cause.

## How the early attributions were set aside

The early search began near the compatibility seam. This term was close to the adaptation boundary, so it seemed like a reasonable direction at the time, but no saved input showed that it had changed the current revision. Someone then shifted attention to wire framing, on the grounds that the object states at the two points in time might have come from different transport handling; there was still no original snippet linking this direction to the discrepancy. The handler registry was also examined, but that only showed that the registration relationships had been checked, not that they had changed.

These directions were later downgraded back to working hypotheses. They are retained to explain why the review had moved through these areas; they are not written up as "the root cause is…" because the current entry point has not provided enough evidence. In particular, the terms that were searched must not be turned into a complete internal call chain. There are no definitive records here of endpoint resolution, a CM session, or other deeper processes.

Another early claim was that the caller's input itself definitely had a problem. This claim was close to the immediate context, so it was easy to accept at first, but it could not explain why the same call relationship could recover at another point in time, and no original record showed that the input object had been replaced. After review, this claim was retained only as an early hypothesis, no longer as a conclusion in the impact assessment. What can be confirmed is that the input and result had, at one point, needed to be saved side by side; it cannot be confirmed that the input was the layer that caused the discrepancy.

There was also a simplified claim: once the page showed green again, the incident could be closed. That is only appropriate as a description of a single occasion when a path returned a usable result, not of the entire anomaly. The green output did not erase the fact that two current revision values had appeared side by side earlier, nor did it turn the recovery action into confirmation of the root cause. Precisely because these two points in time had different meanings, the time of recovery and the time of cause confirmation were not merged.

## Originals, entry point, and recovery page

The original records were not overwritten by the page compiled later. The page's final value can serve as corroborating evidence, but it cannot replace the initial observation; if only the final value is retained, readers will see a clean page but will not know that the integration feedback had once been impossible to reconcile. If only the first screenshot is retained, they will not be able to see that the user path was later restored. The two pieces of material serve different purposes, and neither can be selected as the sole representation of the state.

The role of the entry-point file also has limits. Opening `docs/adj-steamkit2/incidents/SteamKit2-client-integration-same-object-two-states.md` takes you back to the original record for this adj-steamkit2 incident-export. It tells readers where to start looking, not which of the two revisions is correct. Paths, attachments, and observations of the objects must be retained together; the entry-point file cannot be interpreted as the source of the change simply because it still exists.

Retracing the original input during the review can only confirm what the current entry point has already exposed. Branches that were not reproduced were not filled in with actions attributed to some neighboring component, nor was a successful retry used as a substitute for the failure window. The reason for stopping further retries was practical: obtaining a result again adds another observation, but unless the request context, entry-point version, and corresponding object are retained at the same time, the new and old results cannot be reliably aligned.

The request context was added separately to the handoff. The purpose here was not to add another operations manual, but to avoid looking only at the last line of output. A green response must, at a minimum, be read alongside its corresponding revision, caller sample, and entry-point version; if these objects were not retained together, a green result cannot be used to infer retrospectively that the state was already stable. The source material did not provide specific accounts, commands, or request IDs, so this page does not invent them.

## Conclusions drawn from the recovery actions

Recovery followed a conservative sequence: first preserve the original input, entry-point version, and observed object state; once the call path became available again, append the recovery result alongside the original event; stop speculating further about branches that were not reproduced. This action resolved "whether integration testing could continue afterward", but did not resolve "why the two points in time differed".

Therefore, the recovery results were not placed before the impact description. The impact description first explains how inconsistent object states blocked adaptation decisions, and the recovery section then explains that the user path later became available again. This prevents readers from mistaking "we can proceed" for "there was no earlier impact", or "it did not fail again" for "the root cause has been confirmed".

Retrying until a particular result became stable was not the criterion used at the time. The first record had already shown that the same object could return different current revision values at two points in time, and obtaining a single green result during repeated attempts cannot prove that the state is stable. If an inconsistency appears again during the next incident, the new input and context should be saved and compared side by side with those from the original incident, rather than directly rewriting the first record.

fixture replay was not expanded into a recovery procedure either. The old note mentioned this term alongside the incident, but provided no verifiable input, output, or replay results. Without these materials, it shows at most that replay was considered as an approach at the time, not that replay had already taken place, and it certainly cannot explain why the user path recovered.

## State diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SeenMismatch: First observed two current revision values
    SeenMismatch --> Preserved: Preserve the original record and entry-point version
    Preserved --> Rechecked: Recheck via the current entry point
    Rechecked --> Recovered: Caller path restored
    Rechecked --> Unconfirmed: Branch not reproduced
    Recovered --> Unconfirmed: Root cause still unconfirmed
    Unconfirmed --> Rechecked: A new incident of the same kind arrives
```

The SeenMismatch in the diagram is an observed incident state, not an identification of a particular component. Preserved means the originals are still available; it must not be taken to mean that the correct revision has been selected. Rechecked only means that the parts already exposed have been reviewed via the existing entry point; it does not mean that a full call-chain inspection has been completed. Recovered only means that the caller path is available again and cannot replace the preceding failure records. Unconfirmed preserves the gap between the two points in time.

If a new incident of the same kind arrives, first place it alongside the previous current revision, request context, caller samples, and entry-point version. If only page values are visible, those values must still be treated only as corroborating evidence; if only a green result can be reproduced, that still does not justify closing the issue of the two states having appeared side by side. No future comparison is described here as an action already performed.

## Version differences retained after the recheck

The first version was an incident note. It acknowledged that the anomaly existed and that the original entry point should be preserved and further retries stopped, but it lacked a reliable timeline. It placed user-path recovery, consumer contract, and regression lane in the same paragraph, making the recovery appear more complete than it actually was; missing timestamps were retained as blank entries.

The later revision did not fill in a nonexistent calendar timestamp, but instead separated out the sequence that could be confirmed: first a current revision mismatch was observed, then the originals were preserved, followed by a recheck via the entry point, and finally the call path was observed to recover. The intervening material on callback pump, wire framing, and handler registry was put back under "avenues investigated" and was not distilled into a root cause.

The recheck also corrected two premature judgments: attributing the problem to the input and treating a green result as closure. There was not enough evidence to conclude that the input was definitely faulty; green only indicates that a path was usable on one occasion. The impact window, recovery outcome, and confirmation of the cause were therefore kept in separate places. Unsupported material on fixture replay, endpoint resolution, CM session, stream cursor, pooled buffer, and protocol mask was not expanded further as fact.

## Unconfirmed items

1. Which change between the two points in time caused the current revision to diverge, unconfirmed.
2. Whether the impact is limited to the client / extension samples already saved, unconfirmed.
3. Whether the next call of the same kind will still return two states after the user flow is restored, unconfirmed.
4. The exact start and end times missing from the original record, not filled in.
5. There is not enough material to attribute the change to the compatibility seam, wire framing, handler registry or any other specific layer.
6. Whether the final value on the page and the value observed in the caller's environment came through the same entry point, unconfirmed.
7. Whether the entry-point record was replaced, refreshed or re-exported between the two points in time, unconfirmed.
8. Whether the normal observations of the callback pump are related to this discrepancy, unconfirmed.
9. Why the regression lane changed, unconfirmed.

All of these gaps reflect a lack of before-and-after inputs from the same live context, not the lack of an explanation that can be produced by polishing the wording. The current record does not fill these gaps with adjacent projects, hidden internal actions or unsaved request context. If new samples become available later, only when they include both object state and entry-point material, will it be possible to distinguish between a page refresh, an entry-point change and a change in the object itself; this page does not claim that this comparison has already been completed.

## Object Boundaries and Closure Status

This incident focuses only on caller-side integration testing for adj-steamkit2: actual call samples produced by client, extension, the adaptation boundaries exposed by those samples, and how integration feedback is affected by inconsistent object states. This peripheral project has its own schedule, maintainer and exit criteria, so the recovery results remain in this project's records, rather than being automatically merged into the SteamKit2 core or other peripheral pages.

This page does not list Resources · Compatibility Catalog, Samples · Quality Signal Board or LICENSE · Release Automation as participants. Their proximity in the workspace does not mean that they have been affected by this anomaly. Unless a new live case provides the corresponding object, entry point and result together, this page will continue to record only the scope that adj-steamkit2 has already observed.

As of this write-up, the conclusions that can be reliably cited remain very limited: different current revision values appeared at two points in time; this had blocked the caller's assessment of how to adapt; the user flow later recovered; the original failure window, the recovery outcome, and the unconfirmed cause need to be read side by side. A more detailed attribution has not yet been reconstructed from this incident record.

# Caller Integration Test Window Exit Checklist

Use this checklist when the `steamkit2-client-integration` window is about to close. Use it to record what is still visible at the end, confirm whether the exit actions are complete, and leave the caller project's unfinished work with its own maintainers. The relevant owner signs off on release success separately; this checklist does not certify the release outcome.

## Preserve the earlier state first

The early records had only three local markers: `pooled buffer`, `source order`, and `API surface`. At the time, the state was not to be cleared yet if `source order` appeared, and work was to stop if `API surface` did not appear; the recovery action was left as TODO. That version did not validate the recovery steps in the shared environment. This gap remains open; the later addition of a checklist does not mean recovery can be assumed to work.

The second version split the window into opening and closing. At opening, retain the original input, version, and first visible result, along with one success path and one rejection path from the project itself; at closing, check the artifacts or state of `callback pump`. A log entry saying "success" cannot substitute for the actual state. If temporary diagnostics have changed the state, mark the result as not comparable, return to the original input first, and do not overwrite the originals with cleaned-up green records.

## Window-closing actions

1. Align the current checklist version with the actual replay. The entry point is `docs/adj-steamkit2/release/steamkit2-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. Use only inputs already retained during the window; do not create a separate `steamkit2-client-integration` sample that looks identical.
2. Retain both states in the order they occurred, first confirming whether they belong to the same object. The dual-state check recorded in SK2A-015 is the hold point here; if the objects have not yet been matched up, stop and address that afterward. Do not move on to assessing the release.
3. Check the exit actions, the last visible result, and the exit actions for adj-steamkit2. Seeing `depot manifest`, `protocol mask`, or `directory refresh` only shows that the corresponding material was present in the environment; it does not, on its own, mean the window has closed.
4. Check that `callback pump` is not continuing to generate work outside this window, then remove the temporary bypass. If the state is still changing, preserve it and stop; do not clear the queue first and then guess at the cause.
5. After exiting, retain this project's success path and rejection path. If the rejection path is missing, the window is not complete; if the success path is missing, it cannot be filled in with a different caller sample either.

## Versions and chronological order

In SK2A-002, missing intermediate records for the window checklist were noted; leave the gaps blank to start with. The requirement in SK2A-007 was to replay the original input, so review in this order: retrieve the original records first, then check the results actually retained during the window. Later, issues also arose with dual-state objects and with the current revision not matching the page chronology. The page's final value can only be used as supporting evidence; it must not be retroactively treated as the sequence in which events occurred. The checks in SK2A-020 should come after the original timeline: first establish the order of the current revision relative to SteamKit2 · Client Integration, then look at the value last displayed on the page.

The old version focused primarily on `source order`; `failure boundary` was added later. If there are still unconfirmed relationships outside the current interface, stop at the boundary; do not fold in adjacent projects with similar names. Record `handler registry`, `CM session`, and `evidence packet` only if the corresponding outputs actually appeared during this caller window; if the corresponding outputs are not visible, leave them as unknown. Do not backfill these judgments using the page's last value.

## Handoff after closing the window

- [ ] The original input, version, success path, rejection path, and last visible result are still available for review.
- [ ] Exit actions are complete, the queue is no longer accepting new work, and the temporary bypass has been removed.

# Caller Integration Testing Route Proposal

Discussion has focused on the integration route for `steamkit2-client-integration`. There are two options on the table: continue using `failure boundary` to organize caller integration testing, or split `release train` out on its own. Both remain at the proposal stage, with no start date and no owner assignments that would justify declaring either route in effect.

## Differences between the two routes

Staying with `failure boundary` keeps changes concentrated, and callers can still enter at the original integration-testing point. The trade-off is that the failure exit points in several sections are not exactly the same; if they continue to share one route, it is hard to tell which section to return to when something goes wrong. This approach has not yet been shown to be unworkable. It simply retains the original boundaries, and whether each section's failure exit points can be distinguished in actual call samples still needs to be checked.

Splitting out `release train` would take the release cadence out of the caller integration process. The argument in its favor is not that it is more "complete," but that the two sections already have different failure exit points, and recording them separately makes it easier to retain their respective paths for later review. The objections are practical too: integrators would need to remember another route, and there would be more transition points between the old entry point and the new route. Without enough call samples, the split would just add another layer of naming.

## Points left open at the time

The existing callers of `stream cursor` had not all been listed. One caller already being able to run along the old path could not be taken as evidence that all callers could migrate. An actual integration-testing record was still needed to show which side produced `chunk envelope` and which side consumed it; at that point, all that was known was that the term had appeared in related materials. Its precise boundary was not laid out in this draft.

So the trial conditions went no further than this: first use existing callers to check the failure exit points for both routes, then confirm who uses `stream cursor`, and only then decide whether to split `release train` out. If the checks still cannot distinguish the exit points, keep `failure boundary` and do not document the split as the default path. Whether rollback would simply mean restoring the old entry point was also undecided at the time; first, it was necessary to confirm whether callers already integrated had passed through the new transition points. Otherwise, simply restoring the entry point could leave the migration half-finished.

Related materials are kept under `docs/adj-steamkit2/proposals/unadopted-SteamKit2-client-integration-route.md`; for a partial view from the integration side, see DOC-30. This document preserves the comparison of unadopted routes, the objections, and the unresolved rollback questions. Later implementation results are not to be written back as conclusions known from the start.

# Postmortem: Two-State Anomaly in the Compatibility Directory

There was an unreliable sentence on the old page: `release train differs from the old record`. It described the discrepancy seen first, but did not say where the two values came from or what was done after the discrepancy was seen. This version retains that on-call assessment, but puts it back into the timeline as it unfolded at the time. The record for Resources · Compatibility Catalog still uses `docs/adj-resources/incidents/Resources-compatibility-catalog-same-object-two-states.md` as its entry point; the original record, recovery page, and entry-point version did not overwrite one another.

The initial problem was not a confirmed protocol change, but that the same object showed two states during inspection. This object belongs to a public contract built around proto, and also involves migration records and caller compatibility. The release train looked at it using the old record, while another location looked at it through the current entry point, so the results could not be compared directly. The known impact was that release and compatibility decisions no longer had the same reference; there is no evidence that caller data was rewritten, nor that the main project itself experienced the same anomaly.

## The Old Incident Still in the Record

The early record noted only three things: the release train was inconsistent with the old record; further retries produced no new confirmation; and the recovery page and original entry-point version should be preserved. That version placed the discrepancy near `handler registry`, and recorded the assessment that stream cursor was recoverable. This wording was sufficient for handling during the shift, but insufficient for retracing later, because it placed recovery and attribution next to each other.

Samples reviewed later showed that `callback pump` was still normal. This observation narrowed the scope of the incident, but could not show that the state discrepancy had disappeared, nor could it treat `callback pump` as the source of the entry-point version. The original record contains no evidence directly linking the change in `handler registry` to the current revision, so the old page called it an item to investigate, not the root cause.

This page once interpreted "the same object in two states" as one old record not having been replaced in time. This assessment is now preserved only as a historical judgment. It explains why the release train would first see the old value, but not why the entry point could still show another value after a cold start, nor how the same on-call person could give different expiration actions on the two sides. This old assessment has not been changed into the current conclusion.

## Timeline

| Time point | Observed state | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial divergence | `Resources-Compatibility Directory-The Same Object Has Two States` did not match the old record; the entry point returned a different current revision | Saved the original input, entry-point version, and recovery page; stopped repeatedly retrying against the same state |
| Follow-up review | `callback pump` was still normal, with the anomaly concentrated in the object state and entry-point comparison | First narrowed the scope to Resources · Compatibility Catalog, without writing speculation about neighboring projects into the cause |
| 2026-01-20 10:12 | The job used for review had expired, and the logs could not be retrieved for the time being | This part of the incident became blocked; the timeline was not filled in with missing logs |
| 2026-01-20 10:21 | The scope was confirmed to remain within the object relationship of adj-resources | Kept the original entry point and continued checking against this project's contract and migration records |
| 2026-01-23 15:12 | The incident evidence on hand had expired, and the original review sample could no longer represent the current entry point | Put the investigation item back in its pending position and waited for a new sample, without drawing conclusions from the old sample |
| 2026-01-23 17:21 | A new round of checks began | Re-established the comparison from the object state and entry-point version |
| 2026-02-02 13:41 | The toolchain used for the review was fixed | Subsequent comparisons no longer mixed outputs produced by different toolchains |
| 2026-02-03 09:31 | The two records entered direct comparison, and design differences were listed separately | No longer wrote "the old record differs" directly as "the protocol has changed" |
| 2026-02-03 10:54 | The record showed a comparison in which the same on-call person gave different expiration actions on the two sides | Preserved the context on both sides and did not yet decide which side represented the final entry point |
| Recovery point | stream cursor was recoverable, and the user path was available again | Separated the recovery action from root-cause confirmation; the root cause remained open |

There are two points on the timeline that are easy to merge. One is that the entry point can continue operating, and the other is why the entry point returned a different current revision. Recovery has been observed for the former, while the latter remains unresolved. The recovery page therefore cannot replace the root-cause record, and the green result cannot overwrite the original input.

## How the Misjudgment Was Disproved

The first explanation was that the old record was behind and the release train had merely read an old cache. It once seemed plausible because the old value was still in the record, and the first screenshot did not include the full request context. Later, the cold start and the review in another environment forced this explanation apart: if changing only the cache could solve the problem, the entry point at the two time points should converge under the same conditions; the existing material does not prove that.

The second explanation attributed the change to handler registry. It came from a comparison near the entry point, not from a direct observation. The simultaneous appearance of `handler registry` and the current revision only shows that they were seen during the same stretch of investigation; it does not show that the former caused the latter. This term remains on the historical page, with its status lowered from "possible cause" to "unconfirmed adjacent object."

The third easily confused area is tools and samples. The earliest job had expired and the logs could not be retrieved; later, we waited for a new sample and fixed the toolchain. As a result, outputs left at different times cannot be stitched together as one continuous log. During review, the versions, request contexts, and stop points were preserved separately first, and the object states were compared afterward. The blank sections were not filled with imagined switching actions.

This also explains why "the current entry point gave different current revisions at two time points" remains the core phenomenon on this page, rather than an old description that can be casually edited away. The entry-point records at both time points are real, and the discrepancy itself must be preserved; what remains unconfirmed is which step produced the discrepancy and whether it will recur during caller compatibility checks.

## Impact and Recovery Assessment

The current impact scope falls into three kinds of judgment: when the release train uses the old record as its reference, it will conclude that the object has not changed; checking the current entry point will return another revision; and when callers check the migration records, they cannot determine from the object name alone which state they should follow. Resources · Compatibility Catalog still has an independent schedule, owner, and exit criteria, so this incident did not borrow the main project's schedule to indicate that recovery had occurred.

There is no evidence that all callers failed. The observations so far are that callback pump was normal, stream cursor was recoverable, and the user path could later be used again. There is also no evidence that recovery means the versions have been unified. Here, "recovery" only means that the incident was no longer continuously stuck; the source of the state and the correspondence between the two records still require another review.

The on-shift handling first took three practical actions: preserved the original entry point and recovery page; stopped retrying jobs that had already expired; and, after fixing the toolchain, compared the two records again. The order matters. If the old incident had first been overwritten with organized green output, only the result would be visible later, and it would be impossible to know which revision had been used as the reference at the time.

One approach that was not adopted was keeping only the latest page. It could make search results look consistent, but would remove the difference between the initial divergence and recovery, and would make the different values at the two time points impossible to review. Another approach that was not adopted was keeping only screenshots. A screenshot can prove that one line of output appeared, but cannot preserve the version, request context, or stopping condition; the earlier retelling that contained only screenshots therefore did not continue as the main record.

## Incident Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Old record] --> C{Entry-point comparison}
    B[Current entry point] --> C
    C --> D[Current revisions at the two time points differ]
    D --> E[Preserve original record and recovery page]
    E --> F[Stop retrying expired samples]
    F --> G[Recompare after fixing toolchain]
    G --> H[User path recovered]
    G --> I[Handler registry still unconfirmed]
```

The "recompare" in the diagram does not merge the two records into one. It only means looking at the object, revision, and context together after the conditions have been fixed. If the two materials still differ, both materials should continue to be preserved, with their respective entry points and time points identified.

## What Can Be Accounted for So Far

SK2B-002, SK2B-006, SK2B-009, SK2B-013, and SK2B-017 are the related incidents that this page can navigate to. They concern, respectively, release timing, environment switching, the entry-point value after the window ended, cold-start differences, and reruns in another environment. The cards only help locate adjacent records; this page still takes its own entry point, object state, and recovery page as authoritative.

What can be accounted for so far is: the anomaly occurred; the current revisions at the two time points differ; the old record, original input, and recovery page were preserved; expired samples were not treated as new evidence; the toolchain was later fixed; stream cursor and the user path recovered; and the relationship between handler registry and the state discrepancy was not confirmed.

What cannot be accounted for is: which specific cache, job, or registration action wrote the different revision; whether the different expiration actions given by the same on-call person were caused by an entry-point switch; whether all callers can reproduce the issue; and whether the two records should ultimately be merged. The current material does not provide enough evidence to answer these questions, so "the old record was behind" or "handler registry changed" cannot be used as a substitute for an answer.

This postmortem remains stale useful incident material. It preserves the early misjudgment about attribution, as well as unresolved items that were not removed after recovery. If the source of the state is confirmed later, the corresponding time and original input should be added in a new version; do not go back and rewrite this version's unknowns as if they had never happened.

Finally, two concrete follow-up remain: rerun in another environment using the unchanged source and commands, and record the current revision; clear the local cache and rerun the current entry point, leaving the shared cache untouched for now. If the two outputs diverge again, save the request context, entry-point version, and stopping time, then determine whether the discrepancy belongs to the cache, job, or registration relationship. If the outputs converge, that only means the issue cannot be reproduced under those conditions; it does not justify deleting the old incident.

| T+07 | `callback pump` still normal | Narrow the scope first; do not classify adjacent paths as normal |
| T+18 | The comparison points to `handler registry` | Treat it as the next inspection target, not as the root cause |
| T+31 | User path recovered | Record the recovery separately; root cause remains open |

This sequence was later revisited. The recovery at T+31 can only show that the user path recovered; it cannot show that the object pointed to at T+18 has been verified. The same object appearing in different states at different times also cannot be used to infer the sequence of intermediate switches from the final page value. The addendum for `SK2C-012` therefore required the correspondence between the current revision and Samples to be reordered according to the original times; the final page value serves only as corroborating evidence.

```text
user -> Samples-quality signal console-same object appears in two states -> callback pump -> handler registry
              ^ Only the first change is compared here
```

## Impact Window

Impact first appeared in Samples' own failed samples and regression stratification. When assessing a regression signal, treating the current revisions at the two points in time as the same baseline makes the before-and-after statistics incomparable. There is insufficient material here to provide the number of affected samples, nor is there evidence that all user paths experienced the same state change.

An old retelling containing only screenshots had no account, version, or run id. It can prove that someone once saw an anomaly, but it cannot explain why another path was still normal in the same segment of the record. This failed retelling is retained as one of the reasons the assessment kept changing at the time. Later, versions, request context, and stop conditions were added to the on-call handoff, also to avoid looking only at the final line of green output.

The public records for `SK2C-001` successively noted that the previous execution record had already been marked stale, while the source field for the current result remained empty. This excerpt overturned the working assumption that the latest state on the page was the current execution result. It did not invalidate the recovery itself; it only limited the conclusions we could draw from the recovery page.

## How the Misjudgments Were Overturned

The first view treated the entry-point discrepancy as the main problem. It came from the earliest evidence packet: the old record and the current entry point appeared inconsistent, so the response focused on preserving the entry point, stopping retries, and reviewing the original material. This view was not entirely wrong, but it did not explain the whole situation; it failed to distinguish a change in the entry point from a missing result source.

The second view treated the normal state of `callback pump` as the scope boundary. The observation at T+07 covered only this local object and could not establish that `handler registry`, the user path, and the other regression samples were all unaffected. After the observation targets were separated, `callback pump` was retained as an observed local normal state, but could no longer be used as a condition for ruling things out globally.

The third view treated `handler registry` as the cause. The comparison at T+18 did point to it, but the record contained no stack trace, version source, or reproducible branch. It therefore remained only a "next inspection target". `failure boundary` in the old text was handled the same way: retain the original wording and the context at the time, and do not clean it up into a definitive boundary.

`directory refresh` became another inspection point in a later handoff record. Neither it nor `source order` was proven by the existing material to be an action that caused the two states. The same applies to `protocol mask`. These terms were preserved side by side to retain the change in understanding; linking them into a cause would go beyond this record.

## Recovery Actions and Stopping Point

There were three effective actions: preserve the original input and record the entry-point version; record the user-path recovery time separately; stop further retries on branches that had not been reproduced. When a second reviewer retraced the original input, they confirmed only the current entry point; the unreproduced branch therefore remained under investigation rather than being overwritten by the green result.

From the recovery point onward, the practice recorded by `SK2C-003` was to take the first current revision and not mix subsequent aggregation into it for now. This practice addresses temporal mixing, not the way the current revision is generated. `SK2C-006` additionally required marking the time when the current entry point changed and not directly subtracting before-and-after statistics; this addresses the comparison method and cannot replace root-cause investigation.

The on-call handoff additions included the person handing off, the person taking over, and the time Samples confirmed. Before `SK2C-004` was later confirmed, these items remained incomplete handoff information. They affect who took over the incident at what time, but are not enough to prove that any code path changed.

Contacting the original owner before the deadline and, if there is no response, closing out under the existing exit action was the old handling guidance left by `SK2C-009`. It applies to the exit arrangement at the time; it does not mean the root cause has been closed. The current entry point, recovery page, and original failure window should still be consulted side by side.

## Retained Old Material

This page is a stale incident record, so it does not delete the early repeated terms or old judgments. `wire framing` was once written as a location requiring further review, `chunk envelope` as the source of the change, and later `regression lane`, `fixture replay`, and `CM session` also appeared. They came from field descriptions at different stages and cannot be treated as a continuous design description.

"A cleaned-up green result cannot overwrite the original incident scene" remains the most reliable operational lesson from this incident, but it only constrains the way records are kept. It cannot fill in time points that were not recorded, nor can it turn the recovery page into complete execution evidence. We still do not know what specifically triggered the switch between the two states, nor whether the unreproduced branch can occur again with the same input.

Adjacent issues related to `.github/workflows`, release, the build queue, artifact versions, and the rollback window were not included here. Those objects are not part of the confirmed impact scope of this Samples anomaly. `DOC-39` can serve as an adjacent entry-point record, but its old follow-up wording does not change this page's timeline.

## Follow-up Records Still Open

What must continue to be retained is not a new master table, but several specific gaps: the original context for the current entry point's two returns of the current revision; the complete source of the first result at the recovery time; whether there is a reproducible input difference between `callback pump` being normal and `handler registry` being pointed to; and whether `directory refresh`, `source order`, and `protocol mask` are merely observation points.

Until these materials are complete, review Samples statistics separately by the time of the entry-point change. Do not directly merge the values from before and after recovery, and do not substitute the final page value for the original records. Exit actions may be carried out according to existing arrangements, but this only ends the follow-up window at the time and does not rewrite the unconfirmed cause as a confirmed conclusion.

In the exit window, record what remains traceable when samples-quality-signal is removed from the live setup, not a verdict that a particular release succeeded. Check three things here: the exit action itself, the last observed result, and what adj-samples did for the exit. Sign-off by the relevant maintainers remains outside this checklist.

Earlier records only required noting the last result before finishing. In actual handovers, blank windows and pairs of statuses make it easier to mix up objects, so this update spells out the recording process in more detail without filling blanks with guesses.

## Create a record when opening a window

The entry point is `docs/adj-samples/release/samples-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md`. The knowledge base export is latest-known, and Samples · Quality Signal Board continues to maintain the body and attachments. After opening that entry point, first record the following under this window:

- The samples-quality-signal being handled;
- The statuses already seen, in order;
- The last observed result;
- The planned exit action;
- Which items have no record or cannot yet be determined.

This is not another daily report. SK2C-005 requires samples-quality-signal to keep a separate timeline, with only a link in the daily report; the sequence within the window should stay here. If a status appears only in a processed sample, it must not be backfilled into the pre-exit sequence.

Object names in the record should match samples-quality-signal in the live setup. Do not rename and merge two statuses just because they look similar. The verification required by SK2C-007 is to retain both statuses in the order they occurred and first confirm whether they refer to the same object. If that cannot be confirmed, write "two statuses, relationship undetermined" and continue to retain the last result for each.

## Two checks before exiting

1. **The last result is still there.** Review the last result already retained for this window. If processed results were later generated for tiered regression testing or attribution of unstable signals, a green result in that processed output must not replace the original record. If the original record is missing, stop at this check and do not mark the window complete.

2. **The exit action has a record.** After performing the exit action already listed for this window, write the action actually taken alongside the same record. Record only actions performed by adj-samples here; do not infer from this checklist whether the release succeeded or whether other projects can proceed. If the exit action has not been recorded, "it should already have been removed" is not a substitute.

The sample itself may be retained as a failed sample or included in regression tiering; neither means the exit record is complete. If attribution remains unstable, retain the original status sequence and last result, and leave the explanation for follow-up work. Do not erase traces of failed samples just to make the window look clean.

## When you find a gap

SK2C-010 explicitly requires leaving windows with no records blank. A blank is not a success status waiting to be filled in, nor a time point that can be inferred from adjacent windows. When you find a gap, handle it in this order:

1. Mark whether the missing item is the object, status, last result, or exit action;
2. Preserve what has been confirmed without changing its order;
3. Check the records for the current revision; if there are no records, check with the person on duty;
4. If it still cannot be found, write "cannot determine" and halt window closure.

A specific gap was previously left in SK2C-002: the alternative address for the execution record was not written down. In cases like this, do not treat a similar address as the replacement. If the original address is unavailable and no alternative address is recorded, keep the window open; retain the exit actions you can confirm as they actually occurred, and leave unconfirmed parts blank.

Halting window closure does not mean expanding the scope of the checks. This page does not supply release assessments for other projects or turn unknown relationships into fault attributions. There are still no shared-environment test records for the recovery action, so successful recovery cannot be used as a closure condition. If an exit would remove the only record of the live setup, first back out of that exit step, retain the existing record and window, then wait for a verifiable way to proceed.

## Name the actual person taking over in the handover

When a handover is needed, follow Samples · Quality Signal Board's action routing to confirm who is actually taking over. SK2C-013 requires removing decommissioned groups from the new entry point; an old group name is not proof that the handover is complete. The handover record must include, at minimum, the objects still in the window, the last observed result, the exit actions already taken, and any blank items. That way, the person taking over does not have to treat processed samples as the original live state.

The following cards are for navigation only: SK2C-002 is for gaps involving windows with no records and alternative addresses, SK2C-005 points to the separate event timeline, SK2C-007 points to the dual-status check, SK2C-010 points to missing intermediate records, and SK2C-013 points to the post-trigger handover record. They cannot replace the exit records on this page.

Before closing, reread this window: each confirmed object has a last result and an exit action; each unconfirmed object still retains its status sequence and an explanation of the blanks. You may finish the checks on this page only when the first condition is met; if any unconfirmed objects remain, stop without closing the window.

# content-pipeline Public Entry Point Tracing Procedure

This trace produced a path from the entry point to its actual receiving location, not a map of the repository's directories. It starts at the public entry point in the content-pipeline repository. Whoever takes over should start here, first recording the entry point's name and the context in which they saw it, then looking for a call site that connects directly to it. When there are many search results, don't treat matching text as proof of a relationship.

```text
Public entry point in the content-pipeline repository
              |
              v
        One direct caller
              |
              v
First actual consumer in the team's public entry point maintenance work
              |
              v
   Downstream boundary requiring confirmation from another owner
```

`Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/emsg.h` is a file that was actually opened during the early search. Together with the call name, it served as a search anchor, so it remains in this record. The presence of `steam`, `content`, or similar maintenance wording in the file path only makes the file worth revisiting; it does not automatically make it an entry point or establish maintenance ownership. Anyone starting a review here should return to the public entry point and the call site and check whether they really connect.

"Direct caller" has a very narrow meaning on this page: this trace can connect the call site to the public entry point. A declaration, an object with the same name, or a neighboring directory is not enough to qualify as a direct caller, even if it was the first search hit. If a candidate only shares terms such as `content` or `owner`, record it as a signpost off to the side. Signposts can help with later searches, but should not be drawn into the main path or described as an execution relationship that has actually occurred.

Continue from the chosen call site in one direction only. The goal here is not to collect all callers or list every indirect forwarding point. The handoff needs to let the next person retrace the path from the same public entry point to one confirmed consumer. If speculative alternative entry points, unchecked forwarding points, and same-named files are all listed alongside it, readers won't be able to tell which path was actually followed in this pass. When there are multiple candidates, record the one actually followed and leave the rest in side notes; don't use them to draw conclusions about the main path.

After reaching the next location, don't judge by its name whether it is the first actual consumer in the team's public entry point maintenance work. Confirm that it really receives the entry point passed from the previous step and uses what was passed in this maintenance work. Seeing only matching terms, an existing file, or a possible declaration still leaves you at the search-hit stage. The call site in the code provides the evidence for the connection; the consumer's location shows where that connection first feeds into actual work. Don't collapse the two into a vague "found it."

Keep the raw execution record alongside this path, not ahead of the path itself. Code search answers "where are the call relationships?"; the raw execution record answers "which run and which entry point segment showed us this path at the time?" During review, first pin down the scope using the public entry point and the call site, then use the execution record to cross-check the adjacent segments. Keep only the parts of the record that correspond to this path; bringing in the whole record would mistake the context of a single execution for repository structure.

For the handoff, you can leave four local reference points: the public entry point's name and the context when the search began; the direct call site followed in this pass; the receiving location considered to be the first consumer; and raw execution record excerpts adjacent to these two connection points. Finish by recording the stopping point, rather than filling in a presumed maintainer. That way, readers revisiting this know how far verification went and which step still needs confirmation from another owner.

Files with the same name but no call edge can still be useful. They can suggest another search direction or explain why a location was opened early on, but appearing in an old record does not make them a second consumer. In particular, `Resources/NetHook2/NetHook2/steam/emsg.h` is kept here as search history, not as a permanent ownership designation. If a review still finds no direct relationship from it back to the public entry point, leave it as an anchor and return to the main path, rather than continuing to branch out from the filename.

The first draft placed the file location, actual entry point, and location where maintenance happens too close together, making it easy to read the search starting point as the final entry point. These are now separated: the file is an anchor for revisiting the search, the direct caller is the connection check, and the first actual consumer is where this path first reaches actual work in the team's public entry point maintenance. This separation preserves the local relationships already checked without supplying answers about downstream maintenance boundaries.

If the work continues, first confirm at the stopping point whether the handoff is still handled along the same call path, then decide whether an additional entry point is needed. Don't start building another map from the same-named files in the side notes. One discrepancy during the team's public entry point maintenance window has already been saved separately as DOC-46; this page points to it only when needed to explain the scope of the entry point trace, without bringing in that discrepancy's timeline.
